Having reference to the following despatch published In the Montreal Gazette:

"Ottawa, June 3.-The Government, in answer to the telegram from the Canadian Council of Agriculture, urging that necessary steps be taken to have the powers of the Canadian Wheat Board continued at least for another year, sent a reply promising earnest consideration of the request."
1.	(a) Is it the intention of the Government to deal with the proposal of the Canadian Council of Agriculture by legislation this session, or (b) has the Government power under any existing statute to deal with it by Order in Council, and (c) if so, will such powers be utilized?
2.	Is the Government aware that control of marketing of wheat has been abandoned by the United States Government?
3.	Under the powers given the Canada Wheat Board is it the duty of said Board to secure for ithe seller the highest possible price for wheat in the world market?
4.	Has the marketing of the Canadian wheat crop by the Canada Wheat Board resulted in the farmers receiving the highest market price for their wheat?
5.	Has the marketing of the Canadian wheat crop by the Canada Wheat Board resulted in lowering the cost of flour to Canadian consumers?

1.	The matter is now being considered by the Government. [Legislation will be necessary if the crop for the succeeding year is to be controlled, as was the crop for the past year.
2.	Yes.
3.	It is the duty of the Canadian Wheat Board to secure the best possible market prices for wheat according to prevailing rates in the world market.
4.	Yes.
5.	This is largely a matter of opinion. In order to come to a reasoned judgment, one would have to know what would have been the cost of flour to the consumers if the crop had not been controlled, and what would have been the price paid by the millers for wheat if prices had not been controlled. It is impossible to give an answer to that.

Do I understand that section 2 has been carried?
The /CHAIRMAN: Sections 4 and 5 stand. The other sections, from 1 to 9 inclusive, have been carried.
I was under the impression that section 2 had been allowed to stand. Will fche minister allow me to refer to section 2?

(Mr. Archambault
moves that the committee do now revert to the eonsid'araltion of section 2 of the Bill.

I believe that the minister wishes to treat the committee with fairness and that he is even prepared to accept suggestions made by the Opposition. I am sorry that the minister was not in his seat when I made a few remarks on the Budget. On that occasion I suggested that the exemption in respedt of each child be increased from $200 to $500. Everyone who is Messed with children knows that it costs much more than $200 for the upkeep of a child in these days. I have made an offhand estimate of what it costs for the yearly upkeep of a child of ten or twelve years of age, and the figure which I have arrived 'at is $563.30. Everyone knows that one of the causes of race suicide and voluntary sterility is the high cost of the upkeep of children. If a married man has an income of $4,000 and no children he pays income tax on $2,000, the assumption being that the $2,000 upon which he is taxed is that part of his income which is not absolutely necessary for the ordinary needs of life. On the other hand, if he has children !he needs that $2,000 for the upkeep of his children, so that, as a matter of fact, he pays tax on income that is necessary for the upkeep of his family. I am sure that the minister realizes the unfairness of limiting the amount of exemption of each child to $200. I therefore move that the following clause he inserted immediately after clause 1 as clause 2 of the Bill:
Paragraph (b) of subsection 2 of section one of the said Act as enacted by chapter fifty-five of the statutes of 1919, is hereby amended by replacing the words "two hundred" in the first line of said paragraph by the words "five hundred."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are some difficulties in meeting the suggestion of my hon. friend. One of the chief objections raised by many people to the basis of income taxation as carried on in Canada is that the right to tax is not made sufficiently general and that existing exemptions are higher than they ought to be. It is held' that the burden should be spread to a somewhat further degree so that every citizen would feel to a larger extent that he was contributing to the expense of the country and was interested in proper and economic government. The exemption for children is a provision which applies in different countries. It applies in Great Britain, where the exemption for the first child is, if I remember rightly, $200, with a smaller exemption for each subsequent
child. So that Great Britain's basis of exemption on the score of children is the same as ours for the first child, being less than ours for subsequent children. It must. also be borne in mind that the exemption limit on incomes in Great Britain is lower than it is in Canada. In the United States the exemption is exactly the same as our own, and the initial exemption granted for all incomes is also higher than that of Great Britain. I would point out to my hon. friend that if we were to increase the exemption for children in the manner contemplated it would mean that a man with three children would be exempt from all taxation until his income was in excess of $3,500 a year, and the man with six children would be exempt until his income exceeded $5,000.
He deserves it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Probably he deserves it, but, on the other hand, I think he is likely to be much happier than the man who has no children. The married man who has ten children would have to have an income of $7,000 before he could be called upon to pay five cents to the treasury.

Hear, hear, for
him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a class of exemption of such a character that it would make grave inroads upon the public revenue. It would so tremendously increase our present scale of exemptions that I must ask the committee to reject the proposal.

I suppose my
hon. friend will admit that $200 is not sufficient for the upkeep of a boy of ten or twelve or fourteen years of age.
What were the figures my hon. friend gave?
I could give the details; the total is $563.30. Does my hon. friend want the details?

I have had sufficient experience to be conversant with the details.
An lion. MEMBER: That is why you were smiling a moment ago.

I was smiling because I wondered why my hon. friend (Mr. Arch-ambault) omitted the $63.30 in stating the amount. He would have been more logical if he had asked for exemption to the amount of $563.30.

I heartily support the motion of the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres. I think I have sufficient warranty for speaking on this subject, for I am the father of twenty-eight children. It will be conceded, therefore, that I know what I am talking about. I heard the minister state that the father of three children would have to have an income of 83,500 before he would pay the tax; that the father of six children would have to have an income of 86,000-I may be wrong, but that is what I understood him to say-and that the father of ten children must be in receipt of $7,500 before being taxable. I submit to the minister that a man with an income of $7,500 cannot reasonably support and educate ten children if he is subject to income taxation. It is as much as he can do to bring up such a family, as it ought to be brought up, on that income; and I would supplement the motion of the hon. member (Mr. Archambault) and suggest to the minister that the father of ten or twelve or eighteen children should be entirely free from taxation.
He should receive a bonus.

As seconder of the motion I suggest that if the minister is not disposed to accept it in its entirety he should at 'least make some concession and raise the amount of exemption from $200 to $300. The minister has spoken of similar exemptions that exist in Great Britain and in the United States. I believe, .from what I have read in the press recently, that the exemptions in France are much higher than they are here or in the United States and Great Britain. My hon. friend (Mr. Archambault) suggests a bonus, and I think that bonuses are given in France to the fathers of large families. I have here a copy of The Montreal Gazette of March 9, 1920, on the new inheritance tax in France. In that paper the following appears:
Paris, March 8.-France's new inheritance tax will be a novelty. It will be based upon the principle that the more children man has the less estate should be taxed, and vice versa, the fewer children he has, the more tax should be levied. If a man dies without children, the state will take fifty per cent of his estate. If there is one child, the state will take 33 per cent. If there are two children to toe provided for, the tax will toe 25 per cent. Should there

toe three children the tax will be 18j per cent. In the case of four or more children there will be no inheritance tax. Fiscal experts estimate this new tax will bring in 3,000,000 francs annually.
The French Government statistics show that half the French army in the world war came from families having four or more children. The same statistics show that one family in five has as many as four children. Further, more families whose estates are the largest are not those who have four or more children as a rule.
I 'think the minister should raise the amount to $300; this would be acceptable to hon. members on this side.

Mr. Chairman, I am in sympathy with the amendment drawn up by my hon. friend from Chambly and Ver-oheres (Mr. Archambault). I am surprised that this Government, or any Government, should refuse to encourage large families, and this is a proper means of encouraging large families. We are advertising our country abroad to get immigrants, but after all there is nothing like the Canadian-born. He is preferable to the American, Australian, or even British. The asset we most require in this country is the Canadian-born. The principle embodied in the amendment has existed for all time in the history of nations. I would not care to delve into ancient history, but I might recall to my classical friend, the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), that in the laws of old Rome, Augustus, the Emperor, enacted legislation by which the fathers of twelve children were exempted from all taxation and were given lands out of the public domain. This legislation existed all through the Middle Ages in Europe. It was enacted by Louis XIV in France. Coming to more modern times in America-indeed in Canada -the Government of the late Honone Mer-cier in the province of Quebec enacted similar legislation. Grants were made in our province to the fathers of twelve living children. They were made out of the Crown lands and1 they consisted of 100 acres, if I remember well, to each father of twelve children.
In France, unfortunately, the birth rate has been decreasing for many years. Indeed, one of the regrets of French patriots at the beginning of the war, and before the war, was to notice that each year at least one great city was lost by the falling off of the birth rate in France. What made the apparent superiority of the German nation? In 1870 'Germany had the same population, or about the same population, as France; forty years later Germany had nearly doubled its population. In view of

this appalling result, the patriots of France, laymen, priests, free thinkers and practising 'Catholics, have joined hands of late in' order to promote a higher 'birth rate in the old Mother country. Premiums have been given by wealthy Frenchmen, and by patriots through some of the academies of France to fathers of large families, and the French Government at last has awakened and through its legislation has quite substantially encouraged a higher birth rate by exempting from taxation the fathers of large families.
This is a very important topic. It may not so appear when you consider the amount involved in each individual case, but it is a most vital problem for Canada. We have a large country-a beautiful country. The resources of the country have been hardly scratched. We have the potential wealth within the grasp of our hands, but we have not the population. Should we not by all means promote the growth of a healthy and strong population?
We are advertising Canada throughout Europe. I see in the papers every day that American immigrants are beginning afresh their peaceful invasion of the Northwest provinces. Well and good; I am delighted to hear it. The American immigrant is an excellent immigrant. He understands the conditions in Western Canada perhaps better than any other immigrant in the world, but, after all, the best, the most desirable of all citizens is the Canadian-born. Let us through our legislation encourage the increased birth rate of the Canadian.
I said something the other day to the House which I would like my hon. friends to bear in mind just as an illustration of what a steady increase in the birth rate must mean for Canada. Perhaps it is a little selfish on my part, being a Canadian of French descent, to make boast of the fact, but I do make boast of it because the homage is due to the patriotism of our mothers and grandmothers and to the wisdom of our legislators and clergy. I said, and I repeat to-day, that at the time of the Conquest, or if you prefer, at the time of the cession of French Canada to Great Britain, there were in Canada at most
80,000	people of French blood. In 1840, according to statistics, there were barely
1,000,000 French Canadians in Canada. Today there are in Canada 2,500,000 French Canadians at least, and I do not take into account the French Canadians across the boundary. I am told on the best authority that there are no less than 2,000,000 French Canadians in the United States. If it is true, Sir, that a population will double
every thirty years, I invite your attention, ;Mr. Chairman, to this fact that if our people are God-fearing, as they are and a3 they have always been, if they follow the precepts of the Lord, if marriage is encouraged and divorce discouraged, in thirty years from now, speaking from a French Canadian point of view, and it is not a narrow or sectional point *of view, you will have 5,000,000 Canadians of French descent in Canada. In sixty years that number will again bo doubled, and what is a period of sixty years . in the history of a people? This statement is based on the best authority. Lenoy-Beaulieu, who is known as the highest authority on political economy in Europe, once said that the birth rate of French Canada was simply astounding, and he attributed it to the simple life, to the religious life of my fellow countrymen. I do not speak in disparagement of the other races, I know, as a matter of fact, that in the old families in England the children are numerous. I know, too, that in Ireland and in Scotland children are many. I regret to say, and I base my opinion on what a former president of the United States, the late Theodore Roosevelt said, that in the American Commonwealth they have followed another course, and to-day we have the result of race suicide. By promoting divorce before the c6urts, by living a wild life in the cities, by distracting and luring the farming population from rural life tio the cities, they have abolished the old time-honoured family life, which was the pride of the Pilgrim Fathers. This is a very serious problem, Mr. Chairman, and it has a bearing on this taxation measure. I say to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that he will oe a good Minister of Finance if first lie practises economy, and if second, by the distribution of the taxation in this country, he takes the proper view of this national problem, namely the growth of the Canadian born. By his taxation measure he could indirectly-indeed he could directly- promote the increase of our population.
I have said enough, Mr. Chairman. I am in earnest, and I say toi the Minister of Finance that he will get a halo from this Parliament if he promotes the growth of Canadian-born population in Canada

I want to enter my protest against any change in the law as it is now, or against the acceptance of the amendment as proposed by the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres (Mr. Archam-bault). Tf we were to accept in .all serious-

ness, as of course we should, the arguments and the statements advanced by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat we might sum up those arguments in one sentence-it is the advancing of a plea-perhaps an indirect plea but nevertheless a plea-to exempt from taxation the French Canadians in this country.
Oh, no.
That is practically what it amounts to.
Not at all.

Now there have been many means devised at different times to avoid the payment of taxes. For hon. gentlemen to get up and to deliberately and coolly suggest this way as a means of getting out of paying taxation is to say the least of it somewhat unique.
It is a good way.
That is about what it amounts to.
Try it,

I will leave it to my hon. friends opposite who boast of their abilities along that line. Now in all seriousness, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me we should regard this matter of taxation at least from this standpoint: that the people of this country must realize .that we have incurred a large debt as a result of the war and the lesson conveyed by this taxation is that every person should, as far as possible, get his shoulder under that debt and help to lift it. There is something which I think we should not now entirely overlook in the practical application of the tax. Take in the province of Quebec which is largely a rural province-.that is the most of the population are engaged in farming. I venture to say that very few of the farming population in that province will be affected by the tax as it stands to-day. They are exempted up to $2,000, and if they have five children that means a further exemption of $1,000. If hon. gentlemen opposite will tell me that the farmers in the province of Quebec are enjoying incomes in excess of two or three thousand dollars I will be very glad to hear it. I can assure them that is not the case so far as the farmers of Ontario are concerned, and it is certainly not so as regards my constituency, very few of them are affected by this taxation. I think the exemption on $2,000 is suitable recognition. I think it gogs far enough, and that we would be making a mistake if

we accepted the amendment of the hon. gentleman which I have no doubt is presented in all good faith.

I should like to say that the reason I wish to support the Minister of Finance is, that I am .against .the proposition which is being urged here to-day since it is not the principle which has been adopted in taxation in Canada. It would be all very well if this principle had been discussed in a resolution earlier in the session, but it cannot be used, I should think, by the Minister of Finance as a basis of taxation at the present time. We must be logical. While it is true that people should not be penalized for having children, according to our present idea, nevertheless that is not the basis of taxation, and the Minister of Finance, I should think, has no discretion in the matter. While I am on my feet let me say that a moment's thought will show that if the mere multiplication of progeny had been the Creator's idea He would have arranged, as He does with the lower animals, that parents should have a dozen children a year.
Oh, oh.

This idea of making a sort of market for produce for humanity is to me revolting. Statisticians like the French gentleman referred to by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) all agree that no man can properly bring up more than a certain number of children.
How many?
Eighteen.
It is said that some gentlemen like my hon. friend would be embarrassed with even one.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question?

I do not know that this is a discussion upon which we should waste very much time at this period of the session, and I feel very much hesitancy in even saying half a dozen words because I think the minister said all that was to be said on the question. The,e was very much force in his argument that the man who has the children is the blessed man. I think that as my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) is not present I may perhaps be permitted to quote Scripture to the extent of saying that "Blessed is the man who has his quiver full." The proposition contained in the amendment is also scriptural if it be right that,

"Unto him that hath shall be given"; but it would be a very free interpretation of that passage to say, that we shall remit the taxation of men who have large families and the blessedness that comes from large families. I quite agree with the minister that .a childless home is a frightful thing to contemplate. But I do not know thait my bon. friend from Maisonneuve (.Mr. Lemieux)-to whom one always listens with great interest-helped his argument by some of the statements he made with regard to what the Romans did. I am not disposed to draw many of my ideals in this twentieth century from mediaeval or primitive times. The Romans bad their day, and they went. They wanted large families for the purposes of militarism; and we have had enough of militarism not only in primitive and mediaeval times, but in times far more recent.
I was not very much impressed by my hon. friend's statement as to the passible growth of the French Canadian population in this country. It is a matter of comparative indifference to me what section of our population increases so long as we have laws which are equal and just between all our inhabitants, and which will make good citizens of them whatever may be their racial origin. But my hon. friend went on to say that there are 2,000,000 French Canadians in the United States. Now, in making his estimate of what the French Canadian population will be in the years immediately in front of us, he would also have to be able to predict how many of them will go to the United States. If the movement of the immediate future has any resemblance to that of the immediate past, then the effect of this amendment would be to exempt people from taxation to build up the population of the United States, and that would be a very serious proposition for me to give my assent to.
As a matter of fact I think the whole question can be summed up in this way: That the amendment fails to distinguish between a man's parental duties and his duties to the State. A man's parental duties are primary duties which he ought toi be proud and pleased to discharge, and the more he discharges them the better off he is in the possession of his children. But .a man's duties to the State are entirely different, and to say that he ought to be helped in his parental duties by being exempted from his State duties is a proposition to which I could not honestly give my assent. Our parental duties are, I think,
providentially imposed, and it is a primary duty to see that our sons become good men and our daughters good women as far as it iis in our parental power to bring that about. But our State duties are equally incumbent on us, and I certainly think the present exemption is sufficient.
Amendment (Mr. Archambault) negatived on division.

speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 10-One-quarter tax to be forwarded with return; balance may be paid by instalments with interest, etc.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I desire to move an amendment to clause 10 in respect to the question which was brought up by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis). In the proposals that we are making we want the payment of this tax to be left in such a position that no tax-payer will run the slightest risk of loss by making an immediate return, but he will know absolutely that if he has paid too much he will get it back at once. Under the present law there is a provision for refunds provided in subsection 4 of section 10 in these words:
That the minister may refund any tax or penalty wrongfully or illegally assessed and collected, but no refund shall be allowed because of any alleged error in the assessment, unless application therefor is made within twelve months of the date of payment or penalty.
I do not propose to interfere with that subsection, which is quite enough to look after the situation generally; but in connection with the new provisions the position I think ought to be, that no one need make application -for a refund, hut rather that it is the duty of the department to properly check the assessment and the remittance, and if there has been an over-payment to remit the money without delay, instead of waiting until the individual-who probably would never find out that he has made an overpayment-sends in a claim for a refund. Therefore I propose to move the following amendment as a new paragraph, making it subsection 12:
The returns received by the minister shall be with all due -despatch checked and examined and in all cases where such examination discloses that an overpayment has been made by a taxpayer the minister shall make a refund of the amount so overpaid by such taxpayer except in cases wThere any instalment or instalments are either due or falling due by such taxpayer when the amount of the over-payment shall be applied on such instalment or instalments and notice of said action given such taxpayer accompanied by the payment of the balance if any of the amount overpaid.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: In view of the possibility that a person making out his income tax return might very innocently commit a mistake and come within the penalty clauses, which are rather drastic, I would like to know if the minister will make some provision whereby mistakes made in good faith may be generously dealt with by officials of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The clause
really does not deal with the matter in the way that the hon. member thinks it does, although 1 quite understand his receiving that impression at 'the first glance. The taxpayer does two things; first, he shows what his income is. The amount of his income is something which the taxpayer ought to know; i't is something that the department does not know. The next thing the taxpayer is invited and has to do is to send in the amount of the assessment which he thinks ought to be made upon that income. As regards the making of the assessment, I entirely iagree with the hon. gentleman that this is open to error, and no penalty is provided far that. The penalty is not one which has to do with the amount of the assessment a man makes, because that may be full of errors; it has to do with the statement he makes as to his income which he himself alone knows about. Even as regards his income, if he makes a mistake of only 10 per cent, there is absolutely no penalty. Therefore, he is not asked to pay anything for any mistake which could in any way .arise from the construction of these statutes or from the imposition of conflicting or cumulative taxes. If ia man is honest in stating the amount of his income, there is no penalty. If he is dishonest and makes an improper return on a subject which he alone knows all about, he then (becomes liable to a penalty.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: The understanding is that if the person making out a return puts in correctly, or nearly so, his total income, he is not penalized for any deduction which he may make, and to which he imagines he is entitled. *

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at all.
Having that statement of the minister in mind, I should like to know how that harmonizes With the first paragraph of clause 14.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will deal with clause 14 when we come to it. Clause 10 is intended to cover only the income.

Did I understand the minister to say that a man might make an

error of ten per cent in his income without being liaJble to any penalty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Clause 10 at line 31 reads:
If the amount of the income omitted from his return exceeds ten per centum of the correct income.
That is the first 'time when you have any penalty in the nature of a fine imposed. The penalty there is one-half of the amount of the deficiency.
If the amount is less than ten per cent, 'he has to pay 10 per cent interest per annum?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
There is some penalty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not look on that as a penalty.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 11-demand for additional information.

I do not think this Bill provides for the examination of a person who owes the tax. I do no't know whether it would not be wise to insert such provision in the Bill, as such provisions exist in many statutes. For instance, the law 'in Quebec provides that where a person has in law a right to go into another person's business in order to find out if this person can or cannot pay a certain debt, -the law entitles the creditor to call and examine bis debtor. While I am not ready to say that 'a provision of this kind should be inserted in this Bill, it has been recognized through experience that the most proper, direct and satisfactory manner of knowing a man's business, is to examine him under oath.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The officers of the department are of the view that, up to 'the present time at any rate, they have not met .any difficulty which will require that to :be done. As much as possible, the endeavour is to collect the tax in an administrative way, with as little .recourse as possible to law and consequent legal expenses, and with as little harassment of the taxpayer .as possible. In connection with arriving at the amount of a tax, as long as it is quite clear that the department can get all the information they desire to geb-'and the hon. member will see that that provision is .added this year-and if in addition to that they can check the different sources of information, they can generally do just as well as if they .examined the man.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.

On section 14-penalties for short payments or not making payments:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When we were considering clause 10 I had it in mind that it would be desirable to consider this clause in connection with it, because I did not want to have a penalty for a mistake in the assessment itself visited upon the taxpayer. But I find that this point has already been covered,-not in the first draft, but in the amendments made before the printing of the Bill. It- is provided that if the taxpayer does, not pay the amount, or one-quarter of it, estimated by him as the amount that he ought to pay, he is subject to penalty. Then, under section 14 he is again subject to penalty if he does not pay his taxes as provided by the new section, but he is not liable to penalty simply because the amount that he returns is subsequently found to be incorrect. The question of penalties, therefore, turns entirely upon the subject matter that the ratepayer himself knows all about,-the amount of his income and the amount that he himself says he should pay.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
As I read the section, the
taxpayer is penalized if he fails to make any payment at the time of his return. Suppose his understanding is that he owes nothing and that, accordingly, he makes no payment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If his estimate shows no liability to tax, then there is no liability to penalty.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
He is liable to penalty
" should he fail to make any payment at the time of filing his return."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That means, of course, if there is any payment to make.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: It does not say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon.
member thinks there is any doubt about that, there is no reason why it should not be_ amended. But there must be something to pay; if the taxpayer assesses nothing he is not liable to penalty under this section for non-payment.

In this section the
words " the tax as estimated by him " are used, but there is no such expression in section 10.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The whole of
the work done under section 10 is done by the taxpayer. He makes the assessment, and when we come to the penalty we put in the words " as estimated by him " in order to make it absolutely clear that so long as 210
he pays his instalments as estimated by him he is subject to no penalty.
Is any provision made to cover the case of a man who is out of the country and cannot take care of any of these notices, within the required time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We do not extend the time in individual cases. It is the business of taxpayers who are away for any considerable length of time to have some one look after their returns. But the time is sometimes generally extended; we did this year extend it for a period of one month. There is a provision that the minister may at any time enlarge the time for making an individual return, but we try to get along without any individual extensions of time.

(Subsection (2) of section 10 provides that if the minister suspects that the taxpayer is about to leave Canada he may, " for that or any other reason," by registered letter to the taxpayer, demand payment of all taxes within ten days. If the minister were looking after these things personally I would not have any fear concerning them; but matters of this kind are left to his officers in. the various localities. It may be well to take such action if a man is leaving the country, but it seems to me that the use of the words " for that or any other reason " makes, the provision a rather drastic one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is drastic,
but not as drastic as the similar provision in England, where the length of time within which payment must be made in such [DOT]circumstances is five days, I believe. It is essential that the public revenues should be protected. So far as administration is concerned, this action cannot be taken by an ordinary officer. The matter would be the subject of report to the head office, and action could be taken only by the minister or by the Commissioner of Taxation.
On the report of the officer; it is the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh no; I assure the hon. member that the commissioner is not merely a rubber stamp. Moreover, to what country would a man go in order to avoid the tax? I do not think he would go to Great Britain, where he would find conditions worse. I do not think he would go to the United States where, as I am instructed, they have precisely the same provision.

Subsection (2) provides
that:



Non-payment of the said tax within the specified time shall render the goods of the taxpayer liable to seizure by the sheriff of the city, county or district in which the goods of the taxpayer are situate.
Is it the desire of the minister, by this Bill 158, to amend Magna Chart.a, which says that no citizen can be dispossessed of his property without due process of law?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. member not think that this statute is "due process of law"?

The seizure of a man's
effects without giving him opportunity of placing his case before the court would be due process of law if that law were Lynch law as applied in remote portions of Mexico, or, perhaps, in distant parts of Texas.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid
that I cannot follow the hon. member to Mexico.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 16-retroactive effect of sections of this Act.

I suppose the object
is to enable the minister to recover the sums of past years; but |I understand that he does not intend to apply the penalties for the delays.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct. We have had some clauses which entirely interpreted what the law was. So far as the new clauses are concerned, those that we have been discussing recently as [DOT]to the assessment being made by the individual himself, and the penalties provided for, these do not come into effect this year.

I desire to ask the
minister ia question in regard to the returns called for in this section.
Which section?

This refers to three or four of the sections that come into force at ia certain date. There are many companies whose year terminates on December 31st. A company's year ended, say, on December 31, 1919; the dividends were earned in that year's business, but the annual meeting land the declaration of the dividend do not take place until the books are all audited and the accounts are in for that year. The result is that it is perhaps six or eight weeks after the end of the fiscal year before the dividend is declared. I had a slight argument with one of the collectors in that connection recently, and it

appears to me that it is impossible to estimate the dividend before it is declared, even though it may have been earned. What is the ruling of the department on that point? Is At the intention that the dividend shall be charged to the year in which it is paid or the year in which it is earned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The point is
perfectly well taken. We have cleared up any doubt in the matter by section 3 of the present Bill, which reads:
Dividends declared.shall be taxable income of the taxpayer in the year in which they are declared or voted.

Take the case which
my hon. friend from Brantford has mentioned. The year may close on December 31st and the accounts are made up at a later stage, and as a matter of fact the dividends are only collected in the following year. Would they not he part of the income of the shareholder in that year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The dividends
are only declared when the accounts are made up and when the meeting is held.

The declaration of the
dividend does not create an income; it is the payment of the dividend that makes the income. If my hon. friend is going to take the declaration and not the payment of the dividend I think he will encounter some embarrassment. The income is what the man receives, and the year in which he receives it should he the proper accounting period into which it should enter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I confess I
thought that the trouble really was that companies having earned their dividends were not in a position to bring their hooks down and declare those dividends within the accounting period. I think that the tax ought to be paid, as closely as possible, upon money when it is earned. The dividend is an accretion to the taxpayer during the year it is declared.
No. .

It may he declared payable
in so many months' time.

There is no doubt
that dividends are frequently declared months before they are paid. I am aware of a recent case in which it was four months after the declaration of the dividend before anything was actually received. It is the .time between the declaration and the payment that may cause all the trouble.

Many companies do declare dividends far in advance of actual payment, and sometimes the dividends are not paid in cash but by stock. I knorw of a case where dividends were paid in fully paid-up stock, because there was not the actual cash.
The minister has dealt with thait point.

Stock might not be received until some time after the dividend is declared. I am sorry I was not here when clause 3 was adopted, but it seems to me thait we should have a clear understanding as to whether a stock dividend, which is not money at all, is treated exactly as a cash dividend.

The minister dealt
with the question of stock dividends yesterday, iand the hon. gentleman's point has been covered. I am afraid, however, that the minister's view that a dividend earned is to be credited up to one's income when it is declared may be embarrassing. Suppose a man is engaged at a salary of $5,000 a year and through some mishap he does not receive that amount. He has earned it, but in the settling up of affairs it is found that something has gone wrong and be does not get .that money. Would you tax that as his income? It is the same thing with dividends. A dividend is only an income when a man gets it, I would ask my hon. friend to give some consideration to that point because he may find it a difficult one.

There is a further point. A shareholder may cease to be such between the time the dividend is declared by the board of directors and the date at which it is paid. A meeting might take place in December and the directors might declare a dividend payable on the first of February to all shareholders on record on the 15th of January. In the meantime, between the date of the meeting and the 15th of January the shareholder might, if he chose, dispose of his shares, and in that case I do not see that he should 'be taxable so far as those shares are concerned.
He would get the benefit of the disposal of the shares.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

He might dispose of the
money in such a way that it would bring him no immediate return. He might invest it in some enterprise which might not he profitable at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would like to leave it entirely to the committee. It is a 'question whether the ratepayer should he relieved or not. What we have proposed is entirely in easement of the ratepayer. We have thought it fairer no-t to accumulate dividends. There are cases where dividends are paid that represent dividends for a series of years. A company has been in *such a position that the money cannot be taken from it. The effect of this provision is to prevent a larger penalty being imposed on the shareholders. We have not sought to tax the shareholder on money that he has not actually received. Apart from this clause perhaps three or four years' income would he received in the one year.

Then it surely would
come in the return for the next year if he actually received- it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. Take the case of a company that are in the position of not 'being able to distribute earnings for three years. They had been making earnings each year, hut they were not distributing them because they were required to keep the money in the business. Under this section, when the payment was made, the department would distribute those dividends over toi the proper years when declared, although not paid because they could not *afford to pay them. Apart from that section, when the money was received by the taxpayer, it would be part of his taxable income for that one year, and it would put him in the higher brackets as far as taxation is concerned. It may be that it is '.quite unfair that he should be put in the higher brackets because he has been at a loss in the other years. It would be unfair to place him in the higher 'brackets and the income should be considered as taxable in the year in which the dividend was declared though not paid.

I could understand that if you were dealing with the business profits tax there might be something to be said in support of the proposition, because you are dealing with the operations of a company for a given year. But surely on a *question of dividends there is no room for debate that a man's income is that which he receives. If it is not collected, it remains to his credit and it may he paid to him next year. Suppose I were a shareholder in a company and- I did not collect *my dividend in a given year; I would get it next year, and if I were an honest man I would account for it next year. Surely income is that which a man receives, and if

he does not get it in a certain year, there is no income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no feeling one way or the other. It means more money for the department to accept this suggestion and we want to get all the money we can.
If I can secure unanimous consent, I desire to move that the committee return to the consideration of clause 3, which has been agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I heg to move to amend clause 3 by striking out the last three words of the said clause and substituting therefor the following words: "paid or distributed."

Will my hon. friend
need this section at all? It seems to be specially designed to apply to income of the year that has passed. It appears to me that this clause is not necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is to make it clear.

I think the suggestion of the minister would cover the point I desire to draw attention to. I have known dividends to be declared that were not paid and were not allowed to be paid by the bank. The financial position of the company was such that the bank thought it was not desirable to withdraw the money, and therefore the dividends were not paid. That is the reason why the minister has thought it right to clear up that point, and it appears to me that the words he has suggested cover the case. I think it is quite proper that they should be inserted.
Would it not be well to *use the words "in that accounting period" instead of "in that year" in the last line of subsection 5?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That would
not do.

In connection with the sessional indemnity the accounting period of members of the House who are in business falls, say, in the first or second month rather than at the end of the month of December. This accounting period would run through each day until the 31st January, thus overlapping two years. The rule of the department is that the sessional indemnity should be included in the return for the year in which the return i^ made, but the indemnity has not yet been received , by the taxpayer. In that case it is a hardship, -because a member might send in a
JMr. Fielding.]
return of his taxable income to the 31st January and it might include his prospective sessional indemnity which he might never receive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that by far the greater number of cases are better served as we have it now. There are not many returns made in advance.

I understand that the
Canadian Pacific and the Government have come to an agreement as to a flat rate that is being paid- by the company to the Government yearly, and that it accounts for all the taxes that should be paid by the shareholders of the company as income taxes. Does that agreement apply to other companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no
agreement. The Canadian Pacific pays on the basis of the statute.
I understand the company pay $6,000,000 a year to the Government, is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

I am sorry the minister failed to comprehend the force of my argument. To put the case in another way, take the situation last year; a man in business whose accounting period ended January 31 made up a statement for that accounting period and he included in his return his prospective indemnity of $2,500. But during that year there -were two indemnities. Would he be penalized under this new Act for the omission of the two indemnities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
He received $5,000 for the year, but he could only know of one indemnity; consequently he would only include one indemnity in the return; therefore he would be sending in an- incorrect return.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If a member makes up his return in advance in connection with his indemnity that, of course, is something we cannot object to because we want to examine returns that come in as quickly as possible. But the Act does not require him to. All the Act requires to be done is a return to be made on the income during the past year. He is not to take into consideration anything that may accrue to him in the future during any portion of the year in which he is making his return. You do have a little difficulty, though, in partnerships and mercantile businesses where

the accounting periods differ, and there is an express provision of-the Act dealing with that one particular thing:
A member of a partnership or the proprietor of a business whose fiscal year is other than the calendar year shall make a return of his income from the business, for the fiscal year ending within the calendar year for which the return is being made, but his return of income derived from sources other than his business shall be made for the calendar year.

This Bill leaves the matter in an indefinite shape. The person whose accounting period is not in line with . the calendar year, is in the position if he has an indefinite income from another source, that he cannot include that in his return for the accounting period. I know that the department has rules-it has ruled in my own case-that the amount of the prospective indemnity must be included in the return for the year. Now it is impossible for men in the retail business to balance up their books for the year by December 31, and so come in complete alignment with the calendar year. Consequently they balance up their affairs on January 31 or February 31, as the case may be. Nevertheless they are required by the department to do as I have stated. From my own personal experience that has been insisted on.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ksk him a question. He spoke of February 31; I would like to know to what year he refers?
1 meant to say January 31, or the last day of February.
That is putting it correctly.

I thank the hon. member for correction, but my argument is not influenced by it to any great extent, the point is quite clear. I think there should be a definite ruling on the point even though the case may be an exceptional one. When a member of Parliament is required to include all his prospective income in his return there may be a thousand and one reasons which will militate against his receiving that income. For instance death might occur or Parliament might be dissolved. We know for example that in 1919 there were two sessions in the year. A member might include only his indemnity for the one session and then would be subject to a penalty, under the statute, for sending in.a false return.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Of course generally all these taxation matters are expressed with more or less difficulty, and I
admit that the subject is intricate to a greater or less extent. I think, however, that it is quite clear, from the section I have just read, what the real situation is. At any rate it has worked out very well in , other countries where it has been in force for a good many years. Now let us be quite clear as to how matters stand. In the first instance, what is called for, ordinarily, is a return of income received during the year that is past.
The accounting period.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not the accounting period. Let us forget that for a moment. Under ordinary circumstances the return calls for* the income received during the year that has passed, the preceding year. Now then as to where you have a broken accounting period. Take for example,the case of a business whose accounting period ends on January 31, as the hon. gentleman pointed out. In the case of such a business it would be the duty of the manager of that business, in making his return, to include in it the actual receipts or the actual income of that business down to the 31st of January. Take for example this year: the ordinary taxpayer gives the whole of his income up to the end of 1919 in his return, and he makes that return in 1920. The manager of the business of the class I am referring to, instead of making a return for 1919 only, would base . his return on the accounting period which ended the 31st January, 1920.
I beg pardon, the Commissioner of Taxation tells me that I am wrong, too. I think that should be the case, myself, but I am told that the department, instead of doing that, go further in ease of the hon. gentleman than I would. All that you need do, according to what the commissioner says, is to make a return as of the 31st January, 1919.
I think it should be the 31st January 1920, but apparently that is not the fact. Instead of having to make a return in advance, instead of running the danger of being fined,-as the hon. gentleman is pointing out-for an error in connection with something that may happen in the future, you are apparently allowed to go back as far as the 31st January of the year previous. The section apparently is quite clear, and the commissioner is right, for it says:
-whose fiscal year is other than the calendar year shall make a return of his income from the business for the fiscal period ending within the calendar year for which the return is being made.
Now that ends in 1919.

And what about anything outside of that?

ISir HENRY DRAYTON: As to anything outside of the business he is in exactly the same position as any other taxpayer, he would have to pay on exactly what he received during the year.
Mr. PED'DOW: I still submit that it is confusing in connection with the accounting of any business to require any person in business to make two returns-one return for his business accounting period ending January 31 each year, and another return' for income received outside that business. Take a specific illustration, my own case. My accounting period ends January 31 each year. I was compelled to send in a return for 191$, and I was also compelled to send in another Te'turn and include in the accounting period which ended January 31, 1919, my income of which the sessional indemnity formed part. The department insists upon that. My contention is that only what a man actually receives from all sources in the accounting period should be included. That is my argument.

It appears to me that my hon. friend is contending about a point that is very clear in so far as the Government is concerned. The accounting period that the Government sets ends on the 31st December in each and every year. If the hon. gentleman's accounting period is January 31, he does not make the return for that year at all. The hon. gentleman will have the privilege of holding on to the funds for eleven months if his accounting period. is. the 31st January; but he must make his return for all the money he has received up to the 31st December. Suppose the Parliamentary session were on and he had received the indemnity for November and December he would have to make a return of that in his statement for the year. If the Parliamentary session were on and he received part of his indemnity for, say, November and December, he would have to make that in his return, but his indemnity for January, February, and March would appear in his statement for that year; in other words, he would split his indemnity into two parts. The same prinicple would be followed in regard to any other income, and anything received on the 2nd of January, although belonging to the p>evious year, would be included in the next year's return. I fought that out with the inspector, and it was ruled finally that my returns were correct because I included all moneys received up to the 31st of December.

There is no ground for misunderstanding in that statement of the

situation. But you do not understand the position I am placing before the House. Your accounting period ends on December 31, therefore-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member should address his remarks to the Ohair.

I apologize, Mr. Chairman. My hon. .friend is certainly in error in thinking that the two cases are parallel; they are altogether different; and that is where the difficulty occurs. There are many men in business whose accounting period, does not end on December 31, and if placed in the position which I myself and many others are in, they will find a difficulty in complying with the ruling of the department. The department has ruled that it is necessary to include in the returns all that might be anticipated. I have had to fight out with the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If that is the only trouble, Mr. Chairman, I have much pleasure in assuring the hon. gentleman that it will not occur again. No taxpayer is called upon to anticipate anything in his return.
Except his bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was a mistake made by the department.
I am very glad to have that definite assurance from the minister, which settles my difficulty for all time to come. I can assure the hon. member for Coekshutt-
Hear, hear.
I mean the hon. member for Brantford-	[DOT]
The hon. member for the Six Nations.
-that it is not with the object of hanging on to the money for eleven months longer than I am entitled to that I raised the question; it is merely to have it squared away.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.
On clause 4-income from an estate or accumulating in trust.
My hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) made a motion to amend this section by substituting-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
By substituting the words "paid or distributed"
4 p.m. for the words "declared or voted."
Why was this clause held back; what was the trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Following the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) I endeavoured to draft a new paragraph (c) of subsection (1) of section 3, which I submitted yesterday to the minister. I am not aware whether it has received his approval, but I would like to read it. The effect is to amend clause 5 by adding thereto the following words:
and the following substituted therefor:-
Subject to such regulations as may be made by the minister, amounts paid by the taxpayer during the year to corporations organized and operated exclusively for hospitals, orphan *asjylums, and other charitable purposes, no part of the net earnings of which enures to the benefit of any private stockholder or individual, to an amount not in excess of ten per cent of the taxpayer's net income, as computed without any deduction being made therefrom under the provisions of this paragraph.
I would ask for leave to withdraw the amendment which I previously submitted and to move this one instead.
Previous amendment withdrawn.

Hon. members have long been accustomed to make contributions to good causes, in their own constituencies at least, and they should not be denied that privilege by reason of the operation of the income tax. But if a very large portion of our income is taken from us by taxation we may be denied the privilege of mak'ng charitable donations to various good causes. The intention of the Government, is, I am sure, not to prohibit contributions to charity on the part of hon. members or citizens generally who are charitably inclined, and the minister would be well advised to accept this amendment or a similar one-I am not tied to the words; I have it just now for the first time. The amount of income which may be so contributed has been set in the amendment at 10 per cent. That is a modest amount, because many persons give more than 10 per cent of their income to charitable causes. The effect of tins amendment would be to enable citizens to continue their contributions to certain well-established charitable institutions in their own immediate neighbourhood. I personally have for many years taken a considerable interest in an orphanage. I shall not be able to continue to assist in that work if my income is considerably depleted by taxation, and these charitable institutions will suffer. The people generally should be encouraged rather than discouraged in this connection. There is no doubt that charity covers a multitude of sins.

Charity makes the giver feel better and happier. No money is better spent than that which is contributed to a good cause, the welfare of which the donor has at heart.
I have much pleasure in seconding the motion.

I appreciate the motive of my hon. friend (Mr. Cockshutt) in his advocacy of the amendment when he points out that charity covers a multitude of sins. His argument seems to amount to this: that those who are in a position to contribute to this or that institution shall exercise their judgment as to whether they shall give to that institution or whether they shall contribute by way of taxation to the revenue of the country. For my part, I do not think that any person should be allowed to deduct from his income that which he gives to charity or to any charitable institution and thus escape taxation on that amount. I hold that view just as strongly as some hon. gentlemen hold the other view. Certain taxes have to be raised in this country. Let those gentlemen who are blessed with considerable wealth and who are sensible of the enormity of their sins and transgressions, after paying their taxes, cover up the multitude of their sins by contributing to charitable purposes to such extent as they feel disposed.

The assisting of charitable institutions is not by any means confined to people of wealth. Charitable institutions may be generously assisted by wealthy persons, but as a rule they are largely maintained by persons of very moderate means, -maintained because it is absolutely necessary that they should be maintained.
Persons of small means and big hearts.

Quite so. I do not think we should be carried away with the idea that these institutions are entirely maintained by the rich. If charitable institutions are properly defined in the amendment I think it would be a good thing to allow amounts so contributed to be deducted from the net income for the purposes of taxation.

I am heartily in sympathy with the purpose of the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Cronyn), though I wonder whether he is wise in specifying hospitals and orphan asylums; whether a reference to charities generally would not be sufficient. Then, the minister is to make regulations; I assume that they would define what these charities should be.

In connection with the War Charities Act the Government had to accept the responsibility of determining what were war charities and what were not, so that the duty on the part of the Government of arriving at such a decision is not absolutely new. However, in its general purpose I cordially support the amendment of the hon. member for London.

On this occasion I am absolutely in agreement with my hon. friend frt n Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). Charity, to be worthy of commendation either in this world or in the other, ought to hurt the person giving it. If the State is to see that a man is carefully protected in connection with what he gives away, I cann'ot see where the charity comes in. A case of giving was discussed on one occasion by the Highest Authority. We were told that the rich out of their abundance gave, and they did not seem to receive much commendation. Then a widow came along who had only two mites; these two she gave and she was the one who received the praise. In order to make that gift she had to hurt herself; she had to scimp. I do not put myself up as a man who does it, but I do not want to talk buncombe or 'to listen to buncombe. I repeat that in my view the only charity that is worthy of commendation is charity that hurts. If it does not hurt it is not charity; it is that which is described, as I have just said, by the Highest Authority as giving out of our abundance.
I should be sorry to describe as charity on my part anything that was carefully protected from being taxed by the State. We are living in a period when we should realize something of what the world has been going through. We must be prepared as civilians to emulate to some extent the sacrifices of those who have given to the tune of 60,000 men all that they possessed and were-themselves. That is my view of the question and if it comes to a vote I shall have to take the same course as my hon. friend from Frontenac.

This gives a loophole
to some people who may not desire to pay their taxes. Some man might claim exemption on the strength of contributions, real or alleged, to the Red Cross or the Patriotic Fund or some other charitable institution. I am afraid that there are many people in Canada who would be ready to seek exemption and press their claim, because they had contributed to such funds as these.

My view is that if you adopt the amendment the taxpayer will be given the option of contributing to the State or contributing to charitable institutions. If the contributions could be limited in the future to the same proportion as existed in the past there might be some safety valve; but with my knowledge of human nature I think there would be a grave danger, if the amendment were adopted, that thousands of people, influenced by the idea of making themselves solid for the future might be disposed to cheat the State of their legitimate contributions to the public revenue.

In discussing this matter I see no reason why we should confuse the question of taxation with matters of charity. When it comes to paying other taxes than this particular one there is no consideration of charity. Why, therefore, should we make any distinction between the payment of income tax and municipal, provincial or any other taxes? When we are called upon to pay our municipal or provincial taxes we do not introduce the question of charity as a plea for exemption, and whatever we'may see fit to give to charity has nothing to do with our duty so far as the payment of taxes is concerned. For my part, I see no reason at all why charity should be brought into this discussion, and I feel I must vote against the amendment.

I have had
a good deal to do in soliciting subscriptions for onq.good cause and another in the country whenever charitable and benevolent institutions were being promoted or aided, and my experience has shown me that after 'all the bulk of assistance comes from those people whose income is exempt from taxation for the reason that it is small and barely sufficient for their needs. It is from such people that, to a great extent, contributions come for the upkeep of Churches, charitaible institutions, and other organizations that are supported by philanthropy ; and if you grant this exemption to men whose income is large, you will be met with this argument, by those whose income is exempt from taxation:	"John
Jones has a larger income than mine and he is exempt on his charity, while I am not because I am exempt from income taxation." That is the argument that will be put forward by those whose income is below the exemption limit, and I think it would be unwise to accept this amendment.	,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have a great deal of sympathy with the objects of the hon. member for London (Mr.' Cronyn), but so far I have been unaible to see my way to accept the amendment. I look upon the matter, however, as one entirely for the committee, in whose hands I think it can safely be left. I do not desire to add anything except to make ,an observation or Itwo. I want to be absolutely fair about the matter. It is not a question of the ratepayer electing whether he will contribute to the country or to charity, because the exemption is on the amount of taxable income, and no matter what a man may give to charity ,we exact taxation on his income which varies from 4 per cent, 6 per cent, 8 per cent up to 34 and 56 per cent in the higher registers. My objections to the amendment still stand. I am afraid of difficulty arising, not from charitable persons but from the man who does not like to pay taxes; >and I do not think that in the majority of instances, or indeed in any instance, charity would derive any great assistance from a man of that class. We have all kinds of returns made and there is a great deal of checking that has to be done. Unfortunately, there are people who think it perfectly right to cheat in their income returns, just as there are those who cheat in passing the customs barrier, and if he adopted the motion we would only be giving further scope to such people. In the second place, I (think we require all the revenue which we can derive.

I think it is a mistake to treat this as a question of exempting the individual. It is not a question of favouring the individual; the question is not, why .this man should be exempt and another man not exempt. The real question is whether we are going to do something helpful or something injurious to the charitable institutions of the country. That, in my opinion, ,is the correct view of the question. We have not yet in Canada reached socialism, communism, nationalism or any of the other numerous " isms" that exist to-day. We still do a thousand and one things 'by individual effort in this country. There is a vast amount of good done in Canada every day through individual 'action. A great 'deal of charitable work is not done by'governments, either provincial, municipal or dominion, hut by individual effort on the part of the people; and unless we can encourage this individual effort, the charitable institutions of the country

may suffer. I do not think it is worth while discussing the interests of the individual. We should not look upon the question as one of individual exemption,.but we should certainly ask ourselves this question: Are we or are we not going to help those institutions ;which are doing so much good in the country? If the effect of the new taxation is to put a check on the outcome of generosity on the part of the people towards these institutions, then that is>
a fact well worthy of consideration. I am not pleading for the individual but I am saying a word for the thousand and one institutions throughout Canada which I think ought to ibe encouraged and which might probably be affected by this proposed taxation.

I hope for the good of the country that this amendment will foe voted down. After all, it boils itself down to this: This is a request from the wealth of this country to be exempted from taxation. I have nothing to say against them or what they have done but I want to say that some 400,000 or 500,000 men served for a good many years at a very low price and they .are not coming here asking to foe exempt from taxation. If the wealth of this country is going to fall down unless a certain amount 'is deducted from their taxation and if they are going to withhold their contributions to charitable institutions, so much the (worse for the wealth of Canada. I do not believe they will do that, I do not believe they will ask for exemption and I do not believe the members of this House should exempt wealth when they are not exempting those who served the country at the front.

There are just one or two questions raised that I would like to make clear in regard to the wording of the amendment. It says: "Subject to such regulations as may be made by the minister." That is a phrase very commonly used in other taxation measures. In my mind it seemed that under that phrase the minister could make a regulation, for instance, that in the case of any gift to charity the receipt for that contribution must be attached to the return of the income so that there might be no possible question of fraud, as has been suggested. The addition of the iwoTds ' "hospitals, orphan asylums and other charitable purposes" is due ito the suggestion of the parliamentary counsel that hy using the introductory words you practically define iwhat charitable institutions are under the well known legal rule. The 
minister then would have a definite line to determine what were and iwhat were not charitable institutions. I believe that since the war among people of moderate incomes the practice of "giving till it hurts" has prevailed. I know that in our own city we had this year a general campaign for all charitable purposes and it was a pleasure to note that the man of medium income was giving in proportion far more than the wealthy man. .Some of these men, in discussing at the time their subscriptions said: "We look alt our budget carefully; we know what we have and what we can spare for purposes of this kind; this one campaign is to cover everything for this year; we are going to give every dollar we can but if we are called upon in addition to pay a tax on this subscription we must either deduct that tax from our subscription or we must cut off something else." Of course it may foe said that it would foe a fine thing to deny yourself some other need of living. I do think, however, that an amendment of this kind iwould result, whatever the motive, :in a more hearty support of charitable institutions and I need not add now to what has Jbeen so well said by other hon. members on behalf of *these charities.
, Mr. MeKENZIE: I fully agree with the statement of the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) and others who say this amendment should not foe carried. The tax that anybody pays on his charitable givings is entirely too small to bother with. If a person is willing 'to give to charity I do not think he should he worrying about whether or not he is going to be exempt from the email amount of taxation that would be charged on that contribution to charity. I think it might well foe left to the charitable instincts of the people of this country who support the institutions that must live toy charity, I wish to state most emphatically that I am opposed as a matter of policy to any public institution being dependent on charity. That should not ibe the ease. There are a great many very excellent institutions maintained by charity. In the province from which I come there is a hospital absolutely independent of charity. The provincial hospital is absolutely independent of charity. The support of ithe sanitarium in the province of Nova Scotia is entirely independent of charity. The best form of support for institutions of this kind is to tax the people in the proper way so that those who are in charge of institutions of this kind will never have reason 'to he afraid that suffi-

client money 'will not be raised for the maintenance of the institutions. Those who are dependent on these institutions and those who are running them will have no anxiety as to whether the money will be forthcoming for their maintenance. I am bound to vote for the minister's amendment and to oppose the amendment of my hon. friend from London.

speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that the matter was considered in his absence; the point was brought up by several members. A person is not liable to penalties for anything he does not know. He is not liable for mistakes in his own assessment. He is liable if he makes a misrepresentation as to his income. He is liable to a direct penalty if he makes a mistake of over ten per cent in his income, and that is a penalty which is on the ascending scale. He knows about his income and nobody else dops. He is not liable for errors in the assessment he makes on that income because that is something that any one may make errors in connection with. The penalty merely covers first the misstatement in connection with the income and that means the amount of his own income and not the tax; and second, where the man does not pay, according to the assessment that he himself has made, the amount that he ought to pay.

As I understand it the
clause is at variance with the statement which the minister has just made. Paragraph 8 states:
Any person liable to pay any tax or surtax under this Act who, in the return of the income liable to taxation, makes a return in which he states the income to be less than the true amount-

-shall be subject to the' penalty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
