I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that I have been more concerned with trying to raise the money in the way in which it would perhaps do the least amount of harm and from the class that

can most easily pay it, rather than to finally determine just exactly what those taxes ought to be called. I am of the view, in so far as their name is concerned, that I would pay, and do pay, a great deal of attention to what my hon. friend from Red Deer has to say. I realize that he knows much more about the names of taxes and the general system of political economy than I do. I am inclined to think therefore that probably I will be better able to answer my hon. friend's question when these taxes are better understood after the helpful discussion which I am sure the whole subject will receive at the hands of this committee.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must go a little further in this question, and I shall end, if I have only the support of a seconder, by moving an amendment. These taxes, I repeat, are not " excise " taxes-*
-Some hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
-and I think it is discreditable to the Government, to this House and to the country 5 p.m. that it should go- forth to the world that we do not know what excise taxes are and that we allow this thing to isail under a name which it has no right to bear.
I quoted unimpeachable authority on the question, including Webster's Dictionary.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Of course, I can understand a certain proportion of my hon. friends opposite not having regard to any such authority, but I cannot understand my hon. friend the Minister of Finance not having regard to it. Webster's Dictionary says:
An excise duty is an inland duty or impost laid on articles produced and consumed in a country.
Does my hon. friend pretend for a moment that that definition applies to these taxes to be collected under the schedule as it reads now? As these taxes stand at the present moment a man goes into a retail shop to buy an article, and if it exceeds a certain price he is held up at the point of a revolver and made to pay a tax to the retailer, who for the purpose is appointed, willy-nilly, a tax collector by the Government, and has to pay a license for the honour. That is not an excise duty. I would reinforce myself further by an authority which ought also to carry very great weight with any one dealing with
taxes. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines an excise duty as:
A duty charged on home goods either in the process of their manufacture or before they are sold to home consumers.
The essential feature in the first place about an excise duty is that it can be levied only on home goods. There is no pretence that that is so in the case of these particular duties. I protest for the honour of Parliament and the government of the country that we should call these things by a name which they would reasonably bear. They are not excise duties, and no member of the Government can prove that they are. My hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) has just spoken on the subject, but he has given us no enlightenment. After 1 spoke on the second reading, two of the ablest debaters in the Government spoke,-the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) did not refer to the matter at all; the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), after parodying my definition of an excise duty immediately turned to me and said: "Is that the kind of duty that my hon. friend from Red Deer would put on? Then, there would not be many suits of clothes made in Canada." If my hon. friend were in his place, I should reply to him by saying that he knew very well that it was not the kind of tax that I would impose, and in the second place I should reply to him by saying that the kind of tax that I would impose in the country has nothing whatsoever to do with the true .meaning of the words "excise duties." May I add that in the intellectual sphere I have as much respect for a quibbling sophism of that nature as I have for a mosquito in the domain of nature? The point in debate at that time was what was an excise duty according to the well-accepted meaning of the English language. This Government, by Orders in Council and otherwise, living beyond its mandate, as I believe, has done a number of wonderful things; but it has not yet the power to change the meaning of the English language, and it should recede from the attempt. My proposition is made in very good faith. I gave some illustrations, and I do not want to extend the remarks I made on the second reading further, although what I am saying is absolutely apposite to the point under debate or the chairman would, I know, be on my track. I want to submit in the most emphatic language that I can use that a majority of 26 for a Government which was elected less than three years ago by a majority of 70, is a very precarious and fragile instrument to

stand behind these taxes, but it is a much more precarious and fragile instrument to upset the well-established findings of Webster's Dictionary and the Encyclopaedia Britannica.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I most carefully guarded myself from using a single sentence which would come under your censure, Sir, and the point of order was all the less necessary because I had almost finished what I had to say. I have quoted unimpeachable authority to prove, and I have proved that these are not excise duties. You may call them trade imposts. You may call them " borrowings from the United States," and very bad imitations they are, because they go much further than they do in the United States. I called them "internal tariffs," but what they really are is " sales taxes." They are taxes on men who dare to make purchases along certain lines. I have proved that they are not excise duties, and I defy any member of the Government to upset my proof, unless, indeed, they are imbued to an extent that I do not believe they are, with the spirit of the description that was given of the Centurion of old. The. Centurion described himself in this way. He said: "I also am a man under authority; having soldiers under me; and I say to this man, Go, and he goeth and to another: Come, and he

cometh." But I submit to my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) and to the members of that Government with him, for all of whom they know that I have personally a great deal of respect, that though they have done a good deal of saying " Come " and saying " Go," they should not prematurely, without due thought, say, "Go,", to the English language accompanied by Webster's Dictionary and the Encyclopaedia Britannica.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: If I may intervene, I omitted to move my amendment. I move to amend this resolution by substituting the words " sales taxes " for the words " excise taxes " wherever the said words appear in the said resolution.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I think it
would be well, in considering the amendment, to have before us as many authorities as it is possible to cite on such an important matter. The hon. member has given very substantial authorities in support of his contention that the weird " excise " is not rightly applicable to this particular form of tax. If there be one authority above another that is assumed to be reliable on matters of political economy, it is Palgrave's " Dictionary of Political Economy," and I have in my hand the volume which contains a chapter referring to the excise. I shall not recite the entire article, but the first paragraph of it is clear and explicit and, I think, will form a strong argument in support of the amendment. The definition of the excise, according to Palgrave's Dictionary of Political Economy, page 786, is as follows:
The excise is the name given collectively to those duties which in the fiscal system of the United Kingdom are levied upon commodities produced within the kingdom itself, as distinguished from customs duties which are levied at the ports upon commodities imported from abroad. The word excise (latin excido) signifies etymologically something cut off; as an excise duty may in effect be considered something cut off or deducted, for the benefit of the State, from the price of the article as paid by the consumer. If there were no duty the consumer would pay a lower price for the article. The price, therefore, that he actually pays includes the duty; whence it follows that the duty itself is something deducted or subtracted from

the actual price paid. The price in fact is divided into two parts, one part being subtracted from the whole for the benefit of the State, and the remainder going to the vendor.
>Duties of this character, whether levied on articles produced at home or imported from abroad, were at first equally known as excise duties, but in revenue parlance the word has long been restricted to duties on native commodities, those on foreign articles being known as the customs.
Then, the article goes on to state:
An excise -duty properly so-called belongs to the category of indirect taxes.
This tax is certainly a direct tax, not an indirect one, and in that regard, the word "excise" should not be used. Clearly the authorities on political economy generally are at one in agreeing that the word "excise" is used in contrast with the word "customs" to distinguish duties on articles produced at home from those on articles imported. I think thiat Parliament would do well, in its terminology as well as in its legislation, to follow a well established precedent so far as it iis wise to do so.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: So much a gallon is collected on brandy or whiskey; would my hon. friend not consider that impost as coming under the definition of excise?

speechtext: If the article were manufactured in Canada, it would be excise duty; if imported, it would be customs duty.

Manifestly, then, the amendment of the member for Red Deer must be wrong, in part at least, because he would eliminate the use of the word in its application to those very things that the leader of the Opposition says it may be correctly applied to.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: It is the title that is in part wrong.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: The title I suggest would be a true and accurate title, whether it applied to home produce or to foreign produce.

speechtext:
Nearly tall the goods enumerated in this schedule are domestic made 211
goods. I venture to say that not one per cent of the boots and shoes used in Canada are imported goods. Practically the same applies to hats, men's and boys'; caps, men's and boys'; hoise or stockings, silk; neckties and neckwear. In Toronto a few days ago I bought fifty dozen men's neckties, domestic made goods, none of them sufficiently high in price to come under this provision.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: If all the goods numerated were domestic made, my hon. friend's argument would hold good, but if some are not, clearly his argument fails. If these things are all home-made, "excise" is the proper word, but to apply the word "excise" to imported goods is incorrect. "A rose by any other name would smell as sweet." What the minister wlants is to get his money, and, with certain limitations, I would like to help him get it. But the use of the word "excise" is unhappy. The view taken by the hon. member for Red Deer is, in my judgment, sound, and should be sustained.

speechtext:
These taxes will be no
sweeter and no pleasanter to the person who has to pay them simply because of their being designated in any particular way. My suggestion would be to call this a commodity tax. That expression would have general application and would, I think, meet the situation admirably.

speechtext:
I am sorry
that what is evidently considered by some as an unfortunate use of words on my part has led to all this difficulty. My idea, though, is probably the idea of most of the people who are going to be hit by these taxes.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: "Hit" is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Yes, we are
hitting them; we have to hit them. We have to make a lot of the people understand that the war has to be paid for, just as it had to be won. We have on the one hand the customs taxes-the tariff, which a great many people object to-and, on the other hand, excise duties; that has been



the rough and ready division into which taxes in Canada have fallen. It is true that many definitions may be given of the word "excise." I notice that my hon. friend (Mr. ,M. Clark) relies upon an American dictionary for his definition. I also notice that the American authorities use the same designation in dealing with the same sort of things. But this American dictionary rather leaves the matter open. It defines excise, first, as "any commodity, toll or tax"; second, as "an inland duty or impost levied upon the manufacture, sale or consumption of commodities within the country." On the authority referred to by my hon, friend (Mr. M. Clark), therefore, we can say that an excise taxe is an inland duty or impost levied upon the manufacture,-that is one thing-and upon the sale, -that is another thing-no matter where the article comes from.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Does it say that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
That is what I am saying. The definition does not restrict the application of the word to a duty or impost on the sale of an article manufactured within the country. It is a broad tax. It is a tax upon pursuits; upon the following of certain kinds of sports; upon certain trades.	Some people will
say that these taxes are a tax on certain trades; that it makes people engaged in certain trades act as collectors of public revenue and enforces upon them an obligation to which they were not subjected before. 1S0 that the authority referred to by my hon. friend shows that the use of the word "excise" as it is here used is a proper use. It is also a word which can be used in regard to license tax; exactions for licenses can be termed excise taxes.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: You would not import licenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
That is true,
but I do not think that that has very much to do with the question. Further than that, it is a tax:
-applied to duties or fees levied upon makers of, or dealers in, excisable commodities, and finally to various taxes levied for permission to practise or conduct certain sports, trades, occupations. etc.
The English authority, the Imperial dictionary, goes further in support of my hon. friend's proposition than does the American dictionary on which he relies. The Imperial dictionary says:
An inland tax or duty imposed on certain commodities of home production and consumption, as malt spirits, etc.

But in England it covers many other things. It covers all kinds of taxes that are really interior taxes as against customs taxes. For example, it covers the right to keep dogs, to carry a gun, and to deal in certain commodities. The fact of the matter is that so far as custom is concerned, not only in Canada but also in England, the word "excise" is loosely used to describe any kind of tax that is not a customs tax, and I should have thought this a rather happy word for this particular tax. After all, as my hon. friend points out, "excise" means something cut off, and I am not sure that it is not a good name for this tax.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I do not attach as much importance to this matter as some other hon. members, but it is worth while to be right about it. My hon. friend in quoting the authorities appears to raise a possible conflict between the English and the American dictionaries. He gets a little comfort from the American authority, but I want to warn him that there are certain well known reasons why we cannot afford to deal with Americans. I do not want to repeat those reasons, and if there is a choice we had better take the English authority. The *authority quoted by the leader of the Opposition distinctly shows that an "excise" tax is so called to distinguish it from "customs" tax. But I want to set aside both the American and the English authorities and choose one that is better than *they, and that is, a Canadian authority. We have had a practice of our own. We know in Canada what "excise" and "customs" mean; they mean two distinct things, *and if you want evidence of it, my hon. .friend has a document for which he is responsible and which will be helpful. If he will take up his Estimates he will find that we have one branch of the public servic which is known as excise and another branch known as customs. That has been the distinction all through the history of 'Canada. It is a distinction we all understand, and inasmuch as it is familiar to ah Canadians and has always been followed in this country, we might safely put aside the English and the American authorities and follow the Canadian example. I think the point raised by the hon. member for Red Deer is well taken. While I do not attach the utmost importance to the matter-no matter what we call 'the tax it will be just as disagreeable-at the same time, it is just as well that we should be right. We cannot help if we find years afterwards that our statutes have been wrongly translated,

but in this matter we might very well be right at the outset.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I entirely concur in the opinion of the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) that people who must pay the tax will not lie awake >at night because of anxiety as to what we call it. It may be perfectly true that the political economists of the United Kingdom have use the word " excise " in a restricted sense, but it by no means follows that such has been the case on this continent. In fact, I hold under my hand a definition of the word excise by a high legal authority in the United States-I am referring to Mr. Bouvier's work-in which he defines the word excise in a wide sense. There is no restriction at all as to its application to goods that are produced in the country. And after all why should there be? Ii Parliament in its wisdom sees fit to impose a tax, which you may call a commodity or a sales tax or an excise tax, upon all goods produced in Canada when offered for sale, and upon all goods imported into Canada when offered for sale, is any great violence thereby done to the English language? I might quote what my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's has said, that the Canadian authority is best of all; and if tihe Parliament of Canada in its wisdom sees fit to enact that a tax upon goods sold in this country, whether produced in the country or brought into the country, having paid duties upon importation, shall be called an excise tax, I really do not think that ony one, however much interested he may be in preserving the purity of the English language, could take exception to that course.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I am always impressed by an argument on the part of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, and I also appreciate the ability of the Minister of Finance; but I cannot agree with the statement that this matter is not one of importance to the people. The thing that we have to bring home to the people is the fact that these are new taxes, and they should have a new name. We want the people to understand exactly what the Government is doing, and I think there is importance in that. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance said just now that we must bring it home to the people that they have to pay the money. I quite agree with hi*m, and I have expressed that opinion again and again; but I would bring that fact home most severely to the people who have the most money, and when we turn 211* [DOT]
round and take the other course I want the people to understand what it is that is being done. Now, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister says that no great violence is done to the English language if the Parliament of Canada enacts that this shall be called an excise tax. That was the precise point; what he stated as the Act of the Canadian Parliament in altering the meaning of English words. I cannot describe the proposition as other than one which is startling and takes my breath away. It is not the function of this Parliament to alter the meaning of simple English words. That is all the answer I really need to make to my right hon. friend. It is not the function of this Parliament and still less is it the function of this Government. I question if they have a mandate to govern-indeed the recent by-elections have shown that they have not-but certainly they have no mandate to alter the meaning of simple English words.
In regard to the speech of the hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) -he has come very recently to the study of the dictionary and he was interpreting his definitions as he went along. I am sorry for his own reputation that he stopped to emphasize the word "sold " in one sentence that he read. The sentence referred to articles "manufactured and sold in Canada." He says-mark this-" sold " as well as "manufactured." Is it not apparent to a third form school boy that the word "sold " refers to articles which have heen manufactured and therefore to those which 'have -been manufactured and sold within Canada? The whole sentence refers to the same set of articles. I can only classify his interpretation as I classified an argument from another source a short time ago. Clearly and manifestly the sentence refers to an article "manufactured and sold" in Canada. The Minister of Finance says that the word "excise" is loosely used. There is no possible justification for that statement. The word has been precisely used for a century. When the hon. gentleman says that I based myself on dictionaries it is only because I was dealing with one who was new to financial subjects, and I fortified myself with dictionaries. I had to give him what its meaning was from the knowledge I had possessed from my school days.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I care nothing about these exclamations from hon. gents;

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman says I am doing violence to the history of the country. Why, I am following what the hon. gentleman supported in this Parliament. I am following the language that he used as a supporter of the Government, and a prominent supporter of the Government, in 1918. I am following the legislation which was passed then. The legislation of this year is but an extension of what was done then. There is no difference in principle. Take for example what was done in connection with automobiles and jewelry, where the hon. gentleman is dealing with an imported article directly, where he is dealing with a home article directly and where in reference to both of them the excise tax is precisely the same. Where the article is imported such war excise tax would be paid by the importer and where the article is manufactured and sold such war excise tax would be paid by the manufacturer. I am following just what this Parliament has done and the manner in
IMr. M. Clark.]
which this Parliament has described a similar tax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I think this matter might be considered apart altogether from the question of authority and in relation primarily to what will be of greatest convenience to the public in studying and understanding fiscal matters. One may admit that authorities differ. I think, notwithstanding, the authorities quoted this afternoon are pretty well agreed that the distinction of importance is between customs and excise. The point I should like to make is that in future financial discussions we will have occasion to consider what revenue is being derived from customs, what revenue is being derived from excise, as we have used that term heretofore, and what revenue is being derived from the taxes that are now being imposed for the first time. Without some such separate classification, I am sure my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) will find it difficult to make necessary distinctions clear to the House when he speaks of revenues derived from excise duties as the term has been used heretofore and revenues derived from excise as that term is being used in reference to this sales tax. If words have any use at all it is simply as vehicles for conveying thought and ideas from one mind to another. I would submit to my hon. friend that he will be conveniencing the public and every public speaker in endeavouring to interpret these taxes to a public audience by using words that have a common acceptation without any further definition of them. One hon. gentleman has suggested the words "commodity tax." That would seem to be a general and descriptive phrase by which the meaning could be easily and quickly grasped. When one uses the word "excise" the public mind is going to think of the word " excise " as it has hitherto been used as applied to existing excise duties. If the words " sales tax" were used, the public mind would not suffer confusion when this particular tax is under consideration. I think it will save confusion in the future and make for a clearer comprehension of important differences, if the suggestions made are considered in a broad light and not from the point of view of what position has been taken by one side as opposed to the other.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend (iMr. Mackenzie King) seems to overlook the fact that we have already given parliamentary recognition to the word "excise"

in the sense which it is proposed here. By section 19 of chapter 46 of the Acts of 1918 the word "excise" was simply and unequivocally defined, as a duty levied not only upon articles manufactured in Canada but upon articles imported into Canada and put into consumption.
If we propose to depart from that use of the word now we ought to go back and amend the statute of 1918 in which the ward, as I have stated, was most distinctly used in the sense now attached to it in the resolution. I repeat once moire that (L cannot conceive, nor have I heard of any detriment to the public interest from the use of the word in .that sense in 1918, and equally 1 believe no detriment to the public interest can result from the same use of the word in the legislation now proposed by the Minister of Finance. Customs duties are one thing. Excise duties, whether levied on goods produced in Canada or on goods imported into Canada after the customs duty has been paid, are perfectly plain, perfectly distinct, and this use of the word need arouse no criticism whatever in the mind of any person.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: A point to b, borne in mind in regard to the matter to which reference has just been made is that these duties, whenever they have been collected by the State, have been collected- whether on imported articles or on articles produced at home-from the importer or manufacturer, or the producer; they have not been collected direct from the consumer. There is a real distinction between the method of collection of taxation we have heretofore spoken of as in the form of excise and the method of collection of the taxation that is being proposed at the present time; and if there is a distinction as wide as that it would seem, if terminology can assist us in making the distinction clear, that advantage should be taken of it.

speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mr. iOO'C'RSIHUTT : My hon. friend from Bed Deer is particularly exercised with regard to the words "excise duty," and he says we are really setting aside the English language in using them here. Now the hon. gentleman himself was not so careful in
the use of language as applied to these particular articles in his speech during the Budget debate, if my memory serves me rightly. I would like to ask my hon. friend if he can recall the word that he applied to these taxes during his speech on the Budget? Mr. Chairman, he applied the word "tariff" to these taxes, and that is what he is trying to clear the ground for at the present moment; he wants to bring in the word "tariff" a little later on. My hon. friend stated in his Budget Speech, if my memory serves me correctly, that this was not a luxury tax, that it was not a sales tax, but an addition to the tariff. I think I am right in that; I do not wish to ascribe to my hon. friend anything that he did not say. My recollection is that he stated it was an addition to the tariff and should be so characterized. Now whether the tax is an excise or not it is properly designated in the speech of the Minister of Finance as it has been reprinted and distributed. The heading of that speech is, "Excise and Sales Tax." Whether or not the designation should have been repeated in each particular case I will not say. I think perhaps the minister would have been well advised to have done so because there is something in my hon. friend's contention, and we do not want to have in operation a mis-named tax. However, the heading upon the speech is, "Excise and Sales Tax," which evidently pleases my hon. friend. Therefore it is apparent that whatever in the resolution is not an excise tax-and it is admitted there are some excise taxes in it-is a sales tax, and there you have the whole thing. Now if the minister would repeat the designation in every case that is apparently all that is needed; and apparently all the difference between the two hon. gentlemen, as far as I can see, is that the heading of these articles is "Excise and Sales Tax" and therefore in the resolutions themselves those words should have been repeated to have been absolutely accurate. But surely my hon. friend is not going to condemn the whole thing simply because of the insistence upon a name which when used is living up to the economic theories of Adam Smith, Cobden and Bright, and all those great economists of the past who were great authorities on taxation as well as language, and on language as well as taxation. There is no reason, Mr. Chairman, why any fuss should be made about this characterization. There are a great many more important things connected with this matter than the mere name. Of course there is smething in a name, especially if it is a bad name. The

tariff, with my hon. friend, is a very bad name. Therefore he wants to attach these luxury taxes to the tariff and then condemn them from the start in common with all free traders; but he cannot by any process of reasoning add these taxes to the tariff or make out that they increase the tariff, so far as I can understand the English language. I think if the minister simply employs the words that are printed at the head of his speech in connection with these resolutions I am sure that my hon. friend from Red Deer, who is at all times most reasonable, would not kick about a matter so small as this when at the same time he is getting in use his words "Sales Tax" and the minister is using the words, "Excise Tax." Then all parties will be satisfied for - it will be apparent that what is not covered by the word, "excise" is covered by the word, "sales."

I have only a word or two to say if I may reply to my hon. friend's speech with three-quarters of which I agree entirely. When he described me as saying that this was in its nature an internal tariff I absolutely agree-he quotes me accurately. The reason l! figure that this in its nature is an internal tariff is that just as an external tariff takes so much money out of the consumer's pocket when levied-levied at the sea-shore so this tax takes so much out of the consumer's pocket when applied inland. If something is taken out of my pocket,whether at the seashore or inland, I can. assure my hon. friend I am so constituted that in the nature of things I cannot see the difference in the two operations-I am hurt in the same place. I am perfectly agreed as to his accuracy in quoting me, and I am still convinced of the correctness of my views as to what would be an accurate description of the real nature of this tariff.
Now my hon. friend and another hon. gentleman behind him have referred to the editorial heading of the speech of the Minister of Finance. Well, I am sure the minister will not attach so much importance to the heading of his speech that he would want that to set the seal upon the discussion we are having at the present moment. Where I differ from my hon. friend from Brantford is in this:	He says these duties
may be classified as excise and sales taxes. Now what I do most emphatically wish to point out to my hon. friend is, that as there are excise taxes and as there are sales taxes it is really rather a foolish procedure to ap-
ply the term " Excise Taxes" to what are "Sales Taxes." So that he really made a very strong speech in support of my amendment. I only asked very modestly that the words "excise duties" or "excise taxes" should be changed for "sales taxes" in the resolution which we are now considering, if the tax on clothing, and other commodities mentioned therein is to be collected by the vendor at the time of sale. So that I submit to my hon. friend-for whose intelligence I have as much respect as he has for my reasonableness - that if there are both excise duties, or excise taxes, and sales taxes, in these resolutions, as the first resolution refers only to the sales taxes then let us call them sales taxes and not excise taxes.

speechtext:
I should
like to say a word or two with regard to the method of collection of these taxes. In the main, under the provisions of the resolutions as submitted to the committee, the taxes are to be collected by the retail merchant at the time of sale to the ultimate consumer. While having in mind the question of bringing home to the ultimate taxpayer just what these taxes are going to mean to him, and while there is doubtless something to be said for that argument, nevertheless I think the principle contained in thes eresolutions as to the manner in which the taxes are to be collected is going to bring about an almost impossible situation. I take it for granted that the aim of

the Minister of Finance is to secure revenue, and my judgment, after considering the matter with some degree of care, is that the minister, by collecting in the method that is suggested to the committee at the present moment, is not going to get the revenue that these taxes should produce. There are many reasons for that. So many individual transactions have to be covered in securing a definite sum of money that, in the first place, it will be almost impossible to keep a record of the transactions. In the second place, where there happens to be a man who is in business for himself or employing those who may not want to follow this method of taxation honestly, a means is opened up for defeating the very object of the tax and creating, if I may use the term, almost a generation of that class of people who always like to "beat the Government" if they can. During the past two weeks I took the trouble to inquire closely what this means as regards the work involved on the retailer. I may say at once that I am not in the retail business, and the suggestion I have to make before I sit down, if it hits at any one, will hit at the class of people with whom I happen to be associated. I took what I think would be recognized as a not-above-the-average retailer, a man doing a retail business in a town of 3,000 people where there are seven other retail stores. I found that in one day's business, that man had 807 sales' slips, charge and cash sales, involving sums all the way from one cent up. Of those 807 sales' slips, approximately 100 were for sales that would come under the resolutions and for goods that would be taxable. I submit in the first place that if the department are going adequately to check the sales to see that the taxes are properly collected, they would require to cheek the whole 807 sales. I reduced this as nearly as I could to figures in order to see what this meant for the whole Dominion of Canada. There are upwards of 200,000 retailers in business in Canada; and assuming that this man is an average retailer, and assuming that you could get accountants to check these slips at the rate of 10 a minute, it would take 8,000 people working seven hours a day continuously to do nothing but check the slips, provided that all the slips are checked-and if the department are going to see that all the sales that should be taxed are taxed then every sales' slip, whether cash or credit, should be checked. But if we reduce this simply to 100 sales in that particular man's case, it
would still take 1,000 people to check all the sales' slips of all the retailers in Canada. When that retailer to whom I have referred comes to make out his monthly statement to the department, the statement that he must make out will cover 43 sheets of foolscap paper. If you multiply that by 200,000, you will find the volume of returns that the department will have to check in order to get this sum of money. Besides all this, you, are imposing on the retailer a burden that he should not be compelled to carry. You are putting him in a position in which it is not fair to put any class of man, in relation not only to his customers, but to carrying on his business. I do not wish to weary the committee by going into any more of these details. After carefully reviewing the whole situation and discussing it with men who are themselves anxious to assist in working out some practical method of getting the additional revenue the country must have, I have come.to the conclusion that this is an almost impossible method of collecting this tax. The suggestion I have to pass on to the Government and to the minister is this, that after having modified the details of these taxes, as I have no doubt they will be modified in relation to some of the articles, they should then collect the tax on the specific goods that it is finally determined shall be taxed, at the point of manufacture of the finished article and at the point of importation of the finished article. That method can be worked out so that the department will have an infinitely smaller number of transactions to deal with; they will get more revenue, and they will relieve a deserving class of people in this country of a burden that, I think, should not be imposed upon them. I am not at the moment going to move any amendment; I pass this on simply as a suggestion, and I trust the Government and the Minister of Finance will take it into their very serious consideration.

I am very glad my hon. friend (Mr. Nicholson, Algoma) has raised a question which must have been in the minds of every hon. member who has given serious attention to these taxes, the question of the machinery for the collection of these taxes. It is a most important question. We have, in effect, in power in this country at the present time a Cabinet of lawyers. I wish the Government had in their ranks one or two business men such as the hon. member who has just spoken; because they would have saved the Government from getting into trouble such as they

have got into. I have listened with the utmost care to what the hon. member has said, and he has pointed out some of the difficulties connected with the machinery for the collection of these taxes. What is happening at the present moment in1	regard to	these taxes?
Men in business along certain lines in this city-indeed, this applies to the whole of (Canada-find that they are suddenly compelled, by reason of these proposals, to employ a bookkeeper where they did not need one before. Why? Because they have to keep track of all the sales in connection with the new taxes proposed under this resolution. What is it that we actually propose to do under this resolution? We propose to make almost every retail trader in Canada a collector of Government taxes, and make him pay a license fee for the privilege of collecting those taxes. iHe has been doing his ordinary business, with his ordinary staff, under the principles of freedom, but under the principles of [DOT]coercion, which are the secret and the heart of this taxation, he finds that in many cases he has to put on a bookkeeper. Who pays the bookkeeper? The consumers of Canada. Before we go into any detail in the discussion of these taxes we must get to know what they mean in bulk. It is a fact that business men in Ottawa have already had to employ a bookkeeper where they were previously doing their own business. That bookkeeper, call him what you like, is practically an increase of the Civil Service of Canada. It is true that the Government will not have to pay his salary; his salary will come out of the consumers of Canada. If we go along this line, where shall we get to? I am grateful to my hon. friend from Algoma East (Mr. Nicholson) for raising this question of the machinery of taxation.
I should like to know whether the minister can give us any general ideas, before we go [DOT]into details, as to the machinery by which he proposes to collect these taxes, from Halifax to Vancouver, from the northern seas to the American border.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I am glad to
comply with my hon. friend's suggestion. I will say a word first with regard to the matter that has been spoken of by the member for Algoma East (Mr. Nicholson) and other hon. gentlemen. There is no doubt that it is easy to turn away from the duty that is unpleasant; it is easier to borrow money than to impose taxes; tt is much easier to drift than to row against the stream. It is very much easier for the retail merchant if he is specially protected in connection with this matter, and if there is any way of specially protecting him without loss to the State or inconvenience to the community, he shall be protected. On the other hand, if the economic necessities of the situation demand that he should be conscripted, if you like, in his country's service, then he ought to be conscripted in that service. I am not saying at the moment that that is necessary; I shall be pleased to take this suggestion and every other suggestion that is made into my most earnest and careful consideration. What we want to do is to get a maximum of revenue with a minimum of inconvenience, and a maximum of revenue from those classes of people that can best afford to pay. One of the main objections to most forms of taxation is not only that the taxation itself is passed along, but also that profits are predicated on that taxation. What we all try to get at is a tax which will be borne by the men best capable of paying it, a tax so designed that it will not be possible for the person who should pay it to make

somebody else pay it -for him, and at the same time .to .charge .profits on that tax as part of his expenses. That is the main reason why the burden of collecting the taxes has been placed upon the retailer; that is the main reason why similar action was taken in the United States. We have had very marked drops in prices since this taxation was introduced. Would hon. gentlemen expect similar drops in prices if, instead of the purchaser knowing what the tax was, the manufacturer and the wholesaler had been put in the position of .paying that tax in the first instance .and then charging a profit upon it? So far as collection is concerned, our task is indeed easy; if we put the tax upon the .manufacturer and upon the wholesaler we shall have little or no trouble; we shall get a .larger revenue, .and we shall stop a leak here and there which otherwise would not be stopped. But what about the man on the street? What about the man who makes the purchase? We are trying to think of him; we are trying to work out .something which will bring down rather than multiply costs.. Most taxes .are brought into, the cost figures of the concern and have profits placed upon them. This tax cannot be so treated. Everybody knows what the tax is when called upon to pay it, but he need not pay it unless he wants to. Now, that leaves the very important question for consideration and for ultimate determination whether it is in the public interest to collect the maximum of taxation, or whether we should not, on the one hand, seek revenue, and, on the other hand, seek to bring down the cost of .commodities, to bring down the general high cost- of living. Every purchaser should know that when he is buying an unnecessarily expensive article he is paying a little .bit for his extravagance, and is paying to some extent for something that is not an intrinsic quality of the article. We have to consider whether it is worth while that this should be realized. As I have said in connection with *all these resolutions, bearing in mind always the condition of the Country and the fact that we propose to pay our way as we go, to raise proper revenue and, as far as possible, reduce- the high cost of living, all these proposals are submitted to the House in the hope that we may be able maternally to improve our condition. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) has .asked me what concessions it has been thought possible to make in connection with the 'taxes proposed, and I have much pleasure in taking the matter
up in answer to that inquiry. The first taxes which we have are the taxes on boots and 'shoes. There is no question that boots and shoes are an absolute necessity; the only .question Sis that tof (reasonableness of price.

speechtext: Before the minister passes to -a consideration of the individual items, I desire to express my concurrence in the view of the hon. member for Red Deer, that we must first of all knoiw, before we discuss the items, what is the exact machinery that will be employed to collect the taxes. It is now stated in a general way that the taxes should be collected by the retailer. Has the minister realized what it would mean in actual practice for country retail merchants to- collect the duty on (every yard of ribbon that they sell? Let me illustrate (this point. There are five persons in a country store in the morning each of them .seeking to .buy, let us say, a yard or two of ordinary ribbon, which is not a luxury. Some ribbon retails at fifteen cents a yard.

Let us say fifteen cents; that is the average price. The little girls going to school wear this ribbon on their hair, and I do not think you would call that a luxury article. However, the merchant sells, a yard of this ribbon. Do I understand that he is to make a duplicate sheet for the fifteen cents and one for the cent and a half duty he is going to collect, and that he is going to. keep track of that sort of thing from the first hour to the last hour of the day; and that every two weeks or every month, as the case may be, he is going to supply a report to the department? This is one illustration amongst a thousand. If a retail merchant wanted to carry

out the provisions of this resolution he would have to get additional assistance that would entail an expenditure of perhaps a thousand dollars a year. Do hon. members realize what a thousand dollars means to an ordinary retail merchant in a country store? This is a most serious 'question. Cannot the minister find a way to collect through the wholesale dealer these taxes on all the articles mentioned in the resolution. The retail merchant in a country town buys a hundred dollars' worth of ribbon from a wholesale dealer in Montreal, say,-who makes an invoice foT $100 and $10 of excise duty. This is collected from the merchant, who can then fix his price so as to cover any loss in connection with the tax imposed upon him. Could not the minister devise some such scheme? I have consulted a good many retail merchants, not in any attempt to prejudice them against the tax, but simply to ascertain their views; and they all to a man agree that it is almost impossible for them, with the best will in the world, to carry out the provisions of this law. As my hon. friend from Red Deer has said, it would require machinery that would be more expensive than the collection of the customs duty in Canada, whereas if the minister could attain the same end through the agency of the wholesale dealer the work would be much simpler. The only argument the minister can advance against collecting the taxes through the wholesale dealer is that he wants every customer who buys one of these articles that are designated as luxuries to know that the country is collecting a tax from him. Is it so important that a man who is in need of a ten-dollar pair of shoes should know he has to pay a dollar on them? I do not want to go into details, but ten-dollar shoes are not luxuries in my district, where so many ordinary workingmen who axe >at work in the forest, in the driving of logs, require boots and shoes that cost from $12 to $14 and $15.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Beland) is entirely in error. If I said what he thinks I did I improperly expressed myself. I did not refuse any discussion or consideration of the method proposed, but on the other hand, I interrupted and said I would be very glad to go into it and personally to give it my best and most carefful consideration. Further than that, I used words to the effect that while it was my duty and the duty of the House as I conceived it to see that the necessary revenues are raised, if this whole talk about raising taxes and paying our way as we go is not idle chatter, it was also our duty to see that these taxes were collected in the very best and most economical way, in the way which would lead to the least friction and place the least burden upon any section or class in the country, be they retail merchants or any other. My hon. friend from Red Deer has asked what is proposed to be done. In the first place what is proposed to be done is to take advantage of every

constructive suggestion which hon. gentlemen are kind enough to make with that end in view. Apart from that, what would ordinarily be proposed to be done, and what will be done, is to arrange through the Department of Inland Revenue, which department already has the matter in hand, for a proper and systematic way of collecting the tax.
Let me say one thing right here. Whatever hon. gentlemen may say, I think that in so far as the great mass of the retailers of the country are concerned, they do not need hon. gentlemen at their elbow all the time telling them what they should do. I do mot believe it is going to require an army of men to look after the tax. I believe the great majority of the retail merchants are anxious to co-operate in the collection of this tax. They told me sto themselves. They take the view that if this is the only way and the best way the money can be got, while they not like it, they are yet prepared to do their bit, and they iare doing their bit. I do not believe they are a class of men who are going to try and see how much they can knock out of the treasury or how much they can filch from Canada. Therefore, I repeat, we are not going to require any great army of men to look after this tax. We ought not to. While my political experience is short I have had a lot of knocking around Canada and my experience of the Canadian generally is that where there is an honest way of doing a thing he does it honestly and that the crooked man is indeed an exception in this country. We do not propose to employ an army of detectives; we propose to have a very limited number of men to instruct rather than to prosecute or intimidate.
The method by which these taxes can be collected is of course .a matter of regulation. It may be that the whole of the taxes can be collected through the medium of the stamp tax, and if they are collected through the medium of the stamp tax there is no necessity for the book-keeper that the hon. gentleman speaks of. As I said I do not want to pass finally upon everything. No one is more conscious than myself of the fact that this is my first session in this House; no one is more conscious than myself that I require instruction even from the hon. member far Red Deer. But, also, no one is more conscious of the fact that revenues have to be raised and that, inasmuch as this is possible, that we can do it. it is the direct duty of this House to do everything it can not only towards the
raising of the revenues but in regard to the method to be adopted for the raising of the revenues, and to assist in the gradual process of deflation which is so greatly to be desired.
The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) says I am dodging the question. Why? The question of the cent and a half a yard on ribbon is something that can only be dealt with by treating it in the way the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) desired it should be dealt with. - It so happens that I agree with the hon. member for Beauce that cheap grades of ribbon should get recognition and that it should not be necessary for the merchant to make a deduction, or a collection, of a cent, or a cent and a half, per yard on ribbon sold. Boots and shoes certainly .are necessities. My hon. friend from Beauce has made an argument in connection with boots of a character which would be entirely unnecessary in view of the changes to be made. Clothing and the different articles which go to make up Coats and the usual attire are also essentials. Representations have been made by manufacturers of boots and clothing, by wholesalers and by retailers. The retailers do not at all occupy any individual position here. They are not objecting iany more fiercely ot any more strongly than are the manufacturers or the wholesalers. The objections are general, there is no question about that, so far as all these classes of people .are concerned.

Hon. members will see that we have included in that list practically everything which would fall within the general description I was dealing with before, that is absolutely essential articles of clothing, in so far as suits, coats, boots and the like are concerned, and we reduce the tax from ten per cent on the full cost to fifteen per cent on the excess.
Then there is a further stipulation in connection with that, which was in the original schedule; that on articles of clothing the prices of material and cost of manufacture are to be combined ffor determining the selling price.
We do not propose any change at all in the tax on articles the purchase of which may be regarded as an extravagance entirely within the control of the purchaser. For example, we do not think it is any hardship for a man to pay a tax on any hat be wants to buy over $5; so we leave on the $5 limit and the tax at ten per cent on the whole amount, Hats, caps, men's socks, neckties, shirts, ladies' hats, ladies' stockings, corsets in excess of $5, kimonas and waists, petticoats,-all these are left just as they were with the exception of what I have pointed out in the suggestion made, because it is entirely a matter of volition

whether a purchaser indulges in an expensive article or not. A good hat can be purchased at less than $5, and if a man wants a cap he can get one for 50 cents or $1, unless he wants a fancy one-and I admit they are chiefly of that class-and then he should be able to get a good one at $2.
Walking sticks were not covered before while umbrellas were, and I am quite sure that hon. gentlemen will agree that they should be included.

So it has been determined to double the minimum on fur coats and make it $200. That action is taken in view of the necessities of the climate and the way in which the cost of furs has gone up,-although I am very glad to be in a position to inform hon. gentlemen that furs will be coming down in price very soon.

I do not- wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but what is the course we are following in this debate? We come to discuss certain specific proposals which were submitted in the Budget Speech,
which were attached in printed schedules to the Budget Speech. Are we listening now merely to alterations which the Government propose to make in those, and are we going to discuss the alterations at a subsequent date, or are we to take the Budget proposals as serious proposals of the Government for Parliament and the people of this country? What are we doing? We have been here for four months; we waited for the. Budget; we have it, and we have it in printed shape. Now the minister is giving us a whole list of alterations in detail. We have not yet settled, as regards committee discussion, the principles of this legislation. Are we listening to a set of alterations upon which we have to recast all the legislation at a future date? I should like to know what the procedure is that we are embarked upon, and I think I am in perfect order in asking that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I hasten to
assure my hon. friend that the Budget is not a joke and that anything that has been done has been done merely to relieve cases where it is thought that a proper case has been made out for relief; that the further changes -and there are not many-are made to include articles of luxury which ought to have been included in the first resolution and which were omitted; that there is no change whatever in the principle of the Budget, which is a tax on expenditure, most of which is avoidable. What we are doing now is this: I have asked for suggestions, and I still think it is a proper thing to do in connection with new and novel legislation to ask hon. gentlemen for constructive suggestions. If I am wrong, then that kind of suggestion is altogether wrong, and all the minister should come down to Parliament for is to1 logroll something through irrespective of what hon. gentlemen may be able to add to his information or lack of information on the subject. Further, what I am doing is endeavouring to answer a perfectly proper question put by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) and I intend to proceed to answer that question.
We also propose a modification in connection with games and spoTts. What we propose to do there is to make a concession in the matter of popular games, such as baseball, lacrosse, hockey and football. We are removing these from the list of commodities subject to the general tax, but a price limit is being applied, so that if any one wants to get anything particularly fancy in connection with these games, some payment by way of taxation will have to be made. '

Then, a limitation is proposed in connection with velvets, velveteens, etc. We find that a lot of material is cheap in price; that it is used largely by people of small means, and that it is not entirely a luxury. We have fixed a price- in that respect; instead of making the whole of these articles taxable we merely s-ay that velvets, velveteens, plush and silk fabrics, selling at a price in excess of -$2 a yard, shall be taxable. Then, instead of all lace and braid being taxable, we say that only lace and braid in excess of 25 cents a yard -shall be taxable, .and ribbon in excess of 50 cents a yard.
A great many representations have been made in connection with carpets. We have had a fairly thorough investigation made since the Budget was brought down as to the cost of carpet materials, the actual cost of manufacture and the actual prices paid, and we propose to double the minimum in that case. subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WATS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I understood that the question before the committee was whether the taxes should be collected through the retailer or through the wholesaler. I hope we shall have that question settled to-night. I do not see what that has to do with the different levies that are to be put on the various articles. I believe that the minister is making an honest effort to raise as much revenue as possible with a minimum of injury to the poor and middle classes, and I will say, having gone home and travelled on the trains, and having been in a. few towns, I am satisfied that there has not 212 '
been any measure in the last five years that has done as much to reduce the cost of living as the present Budget. When hon. gentlemen opposite say that boots and shoes and clothing have not been reduced since the Budget was brought down I think they are making a great mistake. Retailers have told me that the boots which previously sold at $10 have gone down to $7.50 and those Which sold for $12 are now selling at $9.	1 am now wearing a pair of boots-I
am not talking about ladies' shoes-to my personal knowledge they were selling before at $10, and I paid $7.50 for them. I believe that many of the retailers throughout the country have been charging too much, and this will be the means of bringing down prices. speechtext:
I have been waiting for a considerable length of time to say a few words at this stage of the discussion. Several members made the claim that the Budget is responsible for current retail price reductions. Now, as hon. gentlemen who have spoken on this subject to-night have given their impression of the situation from hearsay evidence, possibly the committee to-night will permit me, as one who has had considerable experience and can speak from inside information on the subject as to the real application of this tax, to say a few words on the matter. These gentlemen

might just as well claim that the price reductions that obtained in the months of November, December and January last were induced by the Budget announcement on the 18th of this month as to claim that the reductions made during the past two- weeks, concurrent with the announcement of the Budget proposals, .were made on account of those proposals. Any one who knows even the A, B, C of retail merchandising, either in this country or elsewhere, knows that there are times in the life of any business concern when, for many various reasons, it is absolutely necessary to unload merchandise. This is made necessary from month to month and from year to year. A merchant may be optimistic and his buyers may be even more so than he is. They go to the market months before the merchandise is required for distribution and place their orders. This merchandise is purchased with the idea that the coming season will be normal, and consequently the distribution of merchandise will also be normal. During the past season, no doubt, buyers everywhere purchased merchandise with the expectation of having normal conditions of weather. They bought heavily of a certain kind of boots, a certain kind of ladies suits, dresses, coats and so on, expecting to have a normal, season in the months of March, April and the early part of May. I need not remind the committee that we did not have normal weather during those months of this year, and consequently merchants throughout the country were left with stocks loaded on their shelves. As a result of that condition, in order to unload the merchandise before the season had completely passed, they were forced to put that merchandise on their counters at reduced pjiees. That is the absolute reason for the general price reductions. No doubt there are exceptional oases such as those referred to by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. -Nesbitt) and the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Best). Those exceptional cases are liable to be found at any season of the year and in any year. I do not need to speak from hearsay; I have known of many instances where people in Toronto bought boots at a certain store in the early part of the week and during the subsequent days of the week they found those same boots were advertised at reduced prices for sale on Friday as bargain day. They took the boots back to the store, got their money on Thursday and went back and purchased the boots on Friday at a lower price than they had bought them at earlier in the week. This was not because of any Budget- announcement or
any influence the Budget exerted on market conditions; these are normal conditions from week to week the year round.
A great deal of discussion has taken place in the press, not only of Canada, but of the United States, on the same subject, Hon. gentlemen who have already referred to this Budget as being responsible for price reductions that have been current during the past two weeks might as well say that the Budget announcement in this Parliament was responsible for price reductions in the United States. For instance, a large concern-I will not mention the name, but it will occur at once to any one who has visited Washington or New York-instituted a horizontal or flat price reduction of 20 per cent on everything contained in their warehouse from the topmost storey down to the basement. I ask hon. gentlemen who have referred to the matter-do they claim that the Budget announcement made in this Parliament last week was responsible for the price reductions in Washington and New York? It is absurd to think of such a thing. Those reductions are the normal, regular, legitimate outcome of market conditions that obtain, and the Budget has no more to do with such price reductions than the man in the moon.
The hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Best) intimated that in his constituency there were good merchants and bad merchants. I hope the committee will pardon me if I admit the possibility of that; but are there not, in all classes, professions, businesses and callings, good citizens and some bad ones too? That is a contingency that is admitted, and it cannot be avoided in any class of the community.	.
I do not wish to delay the committee very long at this juncture; but I might remind the committee that the country is at present face to face with an enormous obligation, and the money must he raised to meet that obligation. The Minister of Finance has decided on a certain method of collecting these taxes. It does not meet with my approval and I would suggest some other method, but he is the man in charge of the ship and he is responsible. It is true we can criticise the method, but he has determined to adopt that method and to push it through to a conclusion. I claim, therefore, that it is the duty of this committee to assist him in framing the resolutions and schedules along the best possible workable lines, and I am willing to give him all the information that it is possible for me, with the technical knowledge I possess in that connection, to render.

It has come to a ease of "put up or shut up." We have to raise the money, and if the Minister of Finance has decided that that is the best way in which to raise it, we have no alternative but to submit and try it out. We can criticise or object; but I do not think our objections will amount to very much, because the majority behind the minister will carry the proposals in any ease. Therefore, it is for us to try to adjust the matter along the best possible lines. I know that, as a matter of fact, the retail merchants of this country are, to a man, willing to help the Government in every possible way, not only in adjusting these schedules, but in collecting the revenue. Doubtless this will mean a large expense on them and on the Government under the method adopted by the minister of collecting the revenue. I should like to persuade him to try another method, but I understand that is impossible. I have here a resolution which was presented to the minister by the Eetail Merchants' Association on the 21st May last in the city of Ottawa. I will read just the concluding paragraph which expresses in a nutshell the attitude of the retail merchants of the Dominion. I might add that there were over 200 retail merchants present at Ottawa on the occasion on which this resolution was presented to the minister. The concluding paragraph reads:
We desire in placing our views before you to say that we fully appreciate the many difficulties under which the Government is labouring, but, as Retail Merchants we desire to offer our services, through our Association, in any manner whatsoever whereby we can give to the Government all the information and assistance that may be required regarding the Retail Trade in Canada.
While preserving the right to criticise schedules when finally printed and presented to the committee, I have very much pleasure in offering whatever assistance I can render to the minister, from my technical and personal knowledge of the matter, in framing and completing the schedules to the satisfaction of the committee and the country.

The most important point that has been raised to-night is that with regard to the means by which this taxation is to be col-

lected. I was a merchant for thirty years, -though I am generally accused of being a bloated manufacturer-and I know a little about merchandise. The suggestion of the member for Algoma East (Mr. Nicholson) should receive serious consideration. The minister will avoid a peck of trouble if instead of collecting this tax from 200,000 merchants in Canada he collects it from the wholesaler, the manufacturer and the jobber. I make that suggestion only as a business man. I want to co-operate with the minister, but I want him to think seriously of what has been suggested in this regard. To collect from the fountain head-the wholesaler, manufacturer and jobber- would be cheaper; would be a more business-like method of procedure, and would bring about actual results within the shortest possible time. Now, it has been intimated that the luxury tax is supposed to have the effect of reducing the cost of living, and that we lose that advantage if we cause it to be paid by the wholesaler, manufacturer or jobber. But if it is going to reduce the cost of living in such a way as to bring the prices down below the figures which are taxable, the minister will not get the revenue that he needs. It has been argued that the imposition of these taxes has brought down the prices of several commodities; if so, these commodities are not going to be reached by this luxury tax. But if the tax is paid by the wholesaler, they will be reached. If, therefore, the Government wants to avoid trouble, if it wants to get the quickest and best results, it should have this tax paid at the fountain head of supply, and paid only once; for if you do not do that you are going to have the tax passed down the line; there will be one, two, or three collections on the same goods if we are not careful. Then, another serious aspect of the matter is the opportunity which exists, under the method of collection as proposed, for avoiding the tax. If there are any dishonourable merchants-though I believe there are very few-there is room for evasion of the tax. For instance, a suit which sells at ?45 is taxed, but if the coat is sold to-day and the rest of the suit a week hence, the tax may be avoided. What is the position of the retailer? Twenty-five or fifty per cent of the merchandise sold in Canada is sold on credit; from ten to twenty per cent of it, perhaps more, is sold over the telephone. The retailer becomes responsible for the tax the moment the sale is made. He not only gives credit on his goods; he has to guarantee to the

Government that the tax on those goods is going to be collected. It goes down on his books. Some of it will never be collected. Well then, the result is that the merchant is liable to be out of pocket not only in respect of the goods, but in respect of the tax on the goods. But he is not permitted to put any profit upon the tax, even though it goes on his books and stays there, perhaps, for thirty, sixty or ninety days. I submit that that is not fair to the merchant. When I was in business 1 gave six months' credit to many farmers; accounts were rarely paid within three months. So that the merchant becomes responsible for the tax whether or not he collects it from the customers. The minister will be well advised to avoid this very serious difficulty.
I have only one or two other suggestions to make. The Brantford merchants have sent me a telegram which is in line with what the minister has proposed,-that is, they ask that the tax be paid on the excess, not on the whole value of the goods; they propose also that the tax be increased in that respect, and that a one per cenit tax on all sales be imposed. I do not vouch for the soundness of that suggestion; I do not know whether it is practicable, or even in line with what I have suggested. Then, there is the matter of electric fixtures. The minister has taken into consideration several items that are to be changed. I submit that electric fixtures are a necessity in the homes of workmen in our cities to-day. Surely an electric fixture with two bulbs on it cannot be called a luxury; ye^ if such a fixture costs $5 there is a 20 per cent tax on it, which adds another dollar to the cost. Having regard to the high cost of building and of all kinds of materials that go into the construction of houses, I ask that the minister consider this matter of electric fixtures. I do not ask him to exempt the fancy chandeliers that cost anywhere from $50 to $1,000, but I do say that the cheap chandelier costing from $5 to $10, that is necessary in every workingman's hou e where electric lighting is used, is not a luxury. The matter of furs should be considered; I believe that the minister is doing something in that regard. I have several protests also with regard to the present proposals affecting jewellery. But all these matters are of minor importance compared with the necessity of devising some better way of collecting these taxes. I repeat that the minister and the Gov>-ernment will be well advised if they have these taxes paid by the wholesaler, manufacturer or jobber.

listened with greater pleasure and gratification to my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Gockshutt) than I have this evening, because I find that for the first time I am able to agree with him on an economic subject.
