On motion of Hon. Martin Burrell, (Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue) the House went into committee on the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act, chapter sixty-six of the Revised Statutes, 1906, and to provide,-
1.	That paragraph (k) of subsection one of section nine of the said Act be amended so as to provide that the maximum registration fee on letters and other matter passing by the mails shall be increased from five to ten cents for each letter or article.
2.	That section fifty-two of the said Act be amended so as to provide that the rate of postage on newspapers and periodical publications printed and published in Canada, and issued less frequently than at intervals of one month, and on all specimen newspapers, be increased from one cent to two cents for each pound weight, or any fraction of a pound weight.
3.	That subsections two and three of section fifty-three of the said Act, as amended by section five of chapter fifty-three of the statutes of 190<S, be repealed, and the following substituted therefor:-
"(2) Newspapers and periodicals required to be transmitted by mail within a distance of forty miles from the place of publication, the publication of which is of no greater frequency than once a week, which have a circulation by mail of not more than one thousand copies per issue, and which are published in any city, town or village which has a population of not more than five thousand persons, shall be transmitted free of postage within such area.
"(3) Newspapers and periodicals which are required to be transmitted for a greater distance than is mentioned in the last preceding subsebtion, or the publication of which is of greater frequency than once a week, shall be subject to postage at the rate of one cent on and after the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-one, and until the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-two, and one and one-half cents thereafter, for each pound weight or any fraction of a pound weight, and such postage shall be prepaid by postage stamps or otherwise as the Postmaster General from time to time directs."
4.	That sections seventy-five, seventy-six, seventy-nine and eighty-one of the said Act be repealed, and the following substituted therefor:
"75. All letters and other mailable matter sent by the Governor General or by any min-

ister or department of the Government at the seat of Government, shall be free of Canada postage under such regulations as are from time to time made in that respect by the Governor in Council; and the provisions of any other statute inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, or conferring any greater powers of sending or having sent mailable matter free of postage than are conferred by this Act, are hereby repealed.
"76. (1) Letters and other mailable matter sent by the Speaker or Clerk of the Senate or of the House of Commons at the seat of Government shall be free of Canada postage, and letters and other mailable matter sent by any member of either House at the seat of Government during any session of Parliament shall be free of Canada postage. Provided that. such letters relate wholly to the affairs of such member of the Senate or of the House of Commons Canada, or to official or public business of the Government of Canada, and that all such mailable matter other than letters in their usual and ordinary form relates wholly to the official or public business of the Government of Canada.
"(2) All letters posted for transmission under this section must be franked by the personally written signature of the member of the Senate or of the House of Commons sending the same. All mailable matter other than letters sent under this section may, however, be franked by the facsimile of the signature of such member as well as by his personally written signature.
"(3) If the signature or facsimile thereof of a member of the Senate or House of Commons be employed for the purpose of franking any letters or other mailable matter except those mentioned in the foregoing section, the person so improperly using it shall be liable to a penalty of three hundred dollars for each offence, to be recovered upon summary conviction.
"79. Members of either the Senate or the House of Commons may, during the recess of Parliament, send by mail, free of Canada postage, all papers printed by order of either House."
I suppose the minister will give a general statement of the purpose of the changes?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
In answer to my hon.
friend (Mr. Fielding) I may say that the resolutions practically explain themselves, and I presume that any lengthy discussion of them may perhaps better take place on the second reading of the Bill when it is introduced. But I will make a running comment on some of the sections. The first section is to alter that clause of the old Act which provides for a five-cent registration fee. It is proposed that ten cents shall be substituted. Last year there was a loss of something like a quarter of a million dollars on that portion of the postal service, and this year that will be seriously augmented by the fact that there is an increase in salariss and bonuses, etc., which would probably reach something like $1,500,000.
Will the hon. gentleman say what he means by a loss in the registration branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: There was an actual loss of a quarter of a million dollars in carrying on that special branch of the service.
Is there any other expense beyond that of the extra clerk for registration in each office?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
According to the return which I have here, the expense of 1918 was approximately three-quarters of a million dollars, the total revenue obtained from the fees collected from this service was approximately half a million dollars there being a loss as between revenue and expenditure to the Post Office Department in the administration of the registration system of approximately a quarter of a million. I am afraid I cannot explain at the present moment the details of the practical administration that would put the expenditure up to that figure. Those are the figures that are given to me as to the cost of administration and the revenue, and the loss entailed is something like a quarter of a million dollars. It was proposed therefore to put the fee up to ten cents which is the same as that in the United States and practically the same as in England, although England runs from a smaller figure up to as high, I believe, as forty cents according to the compensation. I might also add that this will be a benefit to, and will be welcomed by, the rural postmasters inasmuch as it will increase their basis of revenue and therefore increase their remuneration.
The next section provides that instead of one cent on papers published less often than once a month, that is quarterlies, and on specimen newspapers, the rate shall be raised from one cent to two cents a pound. I may say that this increase is largely for the purpose of getting a better revenue out of the very large number of specimen newspapers that are sent around through the country, and which are, in effect, a species of advertising by the paper for the purpose of getting new subscribers. I am not aware that there is any very logical objection to the proposed change.
The next section is that dealing with numbers 2 and 3; with the substitution first of all in number 2 of a rate on weekly newspapers which hitherto, within a radius of forty miles selected by the newspaper itself, were allowed to go free. It is proposed now that the centre of the forty-mile range shall be the place of publication. This was designed to overcome what was

previously open to criticism, a newspaper selecting its point in the forty miles between two large cities in Which case it could fake advantage of those two large cities. The object of this section when placed in the old Act was to encourage the very small weekly newspapers throughout the country, and certainly was not intended to be abused in the way I have suggested. Therefore it is proposed in the first place to make the forty miles start froim the actual place of publication, and for those papers that have a circulation of less than a thousand to go free and those over a thousand circulation to pay the same rate that an ordinary newspaper would pay, limiting also the place to a five thousand population to encourage- the* smaller newspapers and not to encourage in any way or to benefit those weekly newlspapers that are published in cities.

Is the place of publication the place where a paper is printed? For example it is customary in certain parts of the country to have the paper printed at some distance from where the editor and the office of the paper are located. There are papers in the province from which I come that have no printing press hut they arrange with the press, perhaps a hundred miles away, to do the printing. The copy is sent to tthat place and the papers already printed are sent back and distributed from the point where the editor and proprietor happen to live. What would happen in such a case as that?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Well, I should think there could not be any doubt about it. It would be the place from which the newspapers are distributed, that is where the editorial rooms are, because under the old Act it is obvious they would not have got the advantage of free distribution, because the radius was forty miles. I assume that the point of distribution would be the place of publication.
The next clause is that which raises the rate of newspapers of more frequent publication than a week-that is of the daily and semi-weekly papers-from a quarter of a cent a ipoilnd up to a cent a pound, going into operation on January 1st next, and one cent and a half on the following January. I may say in regard to this that it wras to be half a cent in Canada some time ago, and for some reason, about which I am not quite clear, it was put down to a quarter of a cent. There are something like 87,000,000 pounds of news-

papers carried in this country at a quarter of a cent a pound constituting about fifty-four per cent of the total weight of mailable matter. The revenue derived from that quarter of a cent is about $290,000 whereas the total revenues are $25,000,000. That is to say, newspapers, which constitute fifty-four per cent of the total weight pay one per cent of the cost, and the department has estimated that it was losing well up towards $5,000,000 a year by carrying newspapers at a quarter of a cent a pound. They are actually out $2,000,000 in the cost of equipment and necessary material-the actual disbursements-and considering this and the different expenses in the way of salaries and other items they estimate that the loss would probably run up to $5,000,000.

Does not the minister think it is a pretty big jump from a quarter of a cent a year until that one cent is arrived at? The newspapers are in trouble now owing to the price of newsprint and other reasons.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I need hardly tell my hon. friend that I hope I have sufficient sympathy with the point of view taken by the newspapers. I am quite aware that they feel their position very difficult at the present time in regard to the cost and difficulty of obtaining newsprint. I will admit that it seems a pretty big jump from a quarter of a cent to a cent- On the other hand I think it is only fair to point out to the House the fact that the Railway Commission has recently given the railways power to raise the rates on mailable matter; and if-as I have no doubt will happen-they raise their rates at least a hundred per cent, even if we made a raise of only half a ce'nt we would be still in exactly the same position that we are in to-day with respect to loss to the department. It should also be pointed out that one cent-even though it may seem big calculated in percentages-will be hopelessly inadequate compared with the expense of carrying the newspapers. Newspapers in United States, as a matter of fact, to-day are charged one and a half cents for their carriage, whereas we only propose to charge one cent. However, in respect to this- which I know is a very debatable matter; several members of the House have already spoken to me and said they would like to discuss it and put their remarks on record -I would -suggest that the subject can be very well discussed at greater length when the second reading of the Bill takes place,

and as to any suggestions the Government, of course, will give consideration whatever may or may not be done.

Is there any legitimate reason in the public interest why all newspapers should not pay the actual expense of transportation? Why should not newspapers, even under a thousand circulation, pay for their carriage and let them charge that cost up to circulation?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have no doubt there are other hon. members who could answer that question. Of course the view of the Post Office Department generally would be, putting it as a matter of principle, that all service should pay for itself. If we did it in this particular case the newspapers would certainly have to pay a vastly bigger rate of increase than we have even suggested. Of course it is not up to that rate now. Then, one is bound to point out that conditions are somewhat different from what they are in the United States, on account of the enormous stretch of country in Canada and the comparative sparsity of the population. I suppose, too, it would be urged by the newspapers that a newspaper is almost regarded as an absolute necessity and as a great educationl factor; and to charge to the extent that my hon. friend suggests would practically, I have no doubt, put a very large percentage of the newspapers of the country absolutely out of business.
Not if they increased their rates. It is a matter of business.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes. It. is a matter of business.

Would it not be possible for the minister, before the second reading of the Bill takes place, to consider the advisability of increasing the distribution from one thousand to two thousand? Perhaps in the western provinces the proposition might meet with the general approval of a large number of the weekly papers, but when you come to the older provinces like Ontario and Quebec you will find that the bulk of the weekly papers have a circulation of from 1,500 to 2,000, and many even more than that. I certainly think the suggestion is worthy of the serious consideration of the minister. I would also call his attention to the fact that he is now increasing the rate on the other weekly papers and magazines, not one hundred per cent, but four hundred per cent. That is a tremendous jump to make, and
I would ask if it is not possible to consider a more reasonable increase at present.

Before the minister
makes his reply I would like to read a statement which I have received from the Graphic Limited, a newspaper published at Campbellton, N.B. The letter is from Mr. H. B. Anslow:
We ask you to press for the substitution of the following for the above section:
"(2) Local weekly newspapers which have a circulation outside their own town or village of not more than 2,'00'0 copies each week, shall be transmitted by mail free of postage within a distance of forty miles of office of publication."
I understand that under the resolution only 1,000 copies are allowed to be distributed. The writer of this letter adds:
The lot of the weekly publisher is yearly becoming more difficult, until many of us will be crowded out and much good work being done by this class of papers will be lost to the Dominion.	[DOT]
I am advised that the publisher of this newspaper will have to close down his business if he is not allowed the higher circulation.

I shall await the Bill as printed before discussing at any length the subject matter involved in this resolution. But at this stage I wish to state that if the Post Office is in need of a larger revenue there are other means than the present one which might be found to achieve that result. Let me say at once, Mr. Chairman, that the Post Office Department before 1896 was an institution not worthy of the time as regards business methods, and huge deficits followed in succession year after year. But when Sir William Mulock took charge he introduced business methods, and we all know with what result. I may say that in his day he thought of establishing the zone system in order to prevent what were merely advertising agencies benefiting by the low rate of newspaper postage. However, he finally concluded that we might perhaps continue the system, but he cut down the waste as much as possible, and succeeded to such an extent that the department soon became conspicuous as a place where sound business methods were practised. I claim no merit when I say that I followed in the footsteps of Sir William Mulock, and that year after year we had surpluses instead of deficits.' We established, I think, a fair rate of postage on newspapers and magazines, and I gave a preference to British magazines and newspapers by barring out the yellow press and yellow magazines from the neighbouring re-

public. I am sorry to say that that system which gave so much benefit to our settlers in the West was abandoned somewhere round 1912. Now, in order to provide more revenue for the Treasury my hon. friend comes before this committee and proposes to materially increase the revenue of the department by cutting down the privileges of the press and by establishing the zone system. If he wishes to get more revenue I would advise him to chop off the heads of useless officers in that top-heavy staff which he has in the various post offices. The population of Canada has not. increased so materially in the past ten years that in cities, for instance, like Quebec the post office staff should be increased from 90 to over 300. In the city of Montreal the post office staff in 1911 was something like 700; I am informed that to-day it numbers over 2,000. I make bold to say, Mr. Chairman, that at least 200 of those employees in the Quebec ofiice could be discharged, and at least 2,000 at the Montreal post office. I am not speaking of Halifax, or of Toronto, or of Winnipeg, but I daresay that there the same wasteful system has been established by the administration of the department.
But this is beside the mark. We are speaking of the new methods which it has been thought wise to introduce in order to increase the revenue. I have no love to waste on the press of Canada, as members of this committee know; but I put my grievances aside and I stand here this evening as an opponent of any tax on freedom of thought. You can tax my shoes, you can tax my vestments, you can tax my investments.-if perchance I have any,-you can tax almost anything I possess; but, Mr. Chairman, do not tax freedom of thought in this country,-and that is what is being done under this proposal. And besides, you are making no distinction between a real newspaper and a sheet which under the name of newspaper does not convey news, does not disseminate ideas, but is merely a medium for certain fortunate firms who are investing their excess profits in advertising their wares extensively before the public. Let me read the protest of a young Canadian author on this subject. It appeared in Saturday Night some days ago and is as follows:
I wish somebody would explain just why the Government of this Dominion is so intent on playing Herod to those luckless infants of arts and letters which lie within reach of its broadsword. At a time when Canada is struggling to express herself through her own distinctively Canadian periodicals, and is doing her youthful 
best to become something more than what the botanists might term an "obligate parasite" on tiie United States, it seems doubly unfortunate that the life of many of our native .publications should be nipped out by a Postal Zone Bill which carries the threat of an increase of 400 per cent.
As my hon. friend from Lambton has just said:
-in mailing charges within a distributing range of 300 miles, and an increase of at least 800 per cent for still wider areas of distribution.
You have there in a few pointed sentences the effect of this legislation which is introduced this evening. You are increasing by 400 per cent and in some cases by 800 per cent your tax on the press of Canada. He continues:
We want to be something more than a backdoor neighbour of Uncle Sam. We want a voice of our own, and a literature of our own. To have these we must have those publications which remain less involved with the crowded events of the hour than is the daily press. Our authors have survived, it is true, without the protection of that respectable copyright legislation which. most countries extend to toilers in the garden of the imagination. They may even survive a cutting down of their home market. But postal impositions which tend to restrict the disseminations of thought to merely sectional dimensions is retrogressive, and .governmental economies which are bound [DOT]to hamper the diffusion of culture are going to prove repugnant to the open-minded Canadian. It may cost a little more in the bulking up of budgets to encourage our magazines instead of sabering them. But they are trying to make themselves worth the cost. And in the end it is money well spent-as our older and wiser neighbour to the south of us discovered before she went through her own low .fever of postal reform.
Arthur Stringer.
Let us put the question on a higher plane, if I may so express myself. This country extends from ocean to ocean. We have been told repeatedly in years gone by that our business is from East to West and from West to East, not from North to South. We have been told that we should be satisfied with interchange of commerce between the various provinces of this Dominion; we have been told that what we need most is a healthy national sentiment from the Pacific to the Atlantic and from the Atlantic to the Pacific. That is a sound p'licy. We must build a Canada in which the man from the East will, on broad issues, think alike with the man from the West. There must be interchange of ideas between those distant provinces. What are you doing by this legislation? By this postal rate you are preventing the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan), .who is an excellent journalist, whose paper I like to read even when it is against me,

[DOT]from sending his newspaper into Eastern .Canada, and papers published in Montreal, papers published in Quebec, papers published in Halifax, will not circulate in the various provinces west of lake Superior. Is that a healthy condition for this country to establish? I ask my hon. friend to pause and to think seriously before putting this legislation through. You are dividing this country; you are creating the very sectional sentiment which every true patriot must combat to the best of his ability. You are complaining of having three political groups. My good friend the hon. member lor Simcoe North (Mr. Currie) carries with him the claymore of his- ancestors whenever he meets the gentlemen who represent the Farmers' party in this House. He complains bitterly about this evidence of a purely sectional group in Canada. He does not want to see those farmers and their farmer associations thinking only for themselves and of themselves. He wants them to be imbued with the thoughts, ideas and principles prevailing in the industrial centres of Ontario. He is not far wrong in that, so far as ideas are concerned.

First of all, I should like to know when I said all this. The hon. member cannot point to a single word that J said this session or last session against the Farmers' group. The hon. member is framing all this up out of his imagination, "but it is so beautiful that I cannot help listening to it.
I must remind my hon. friend that I have been a journalist, and perhaps some stretches of imagination are permissible. But is it not a fact that this legislation is sectional legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: In what respect?
You are going to close the avenues between the East and the West.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
By what provision of
this legislation are we closing the avenues and making the thing sectional?
By creating a zone system and giving them a special rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman read the resolutions, and if so, does he not see that there is no zone system in them?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: : I must say to my hon. friend very confidently that while the zone system was discussed and considered, the idea was abandoned, and there is in the resolution no zone system except the old regulations which obtained even when he was Postmaster General.

I might also say for the benefit of the hon. gentlemaif that when the Bill comes down I will try to take occasion to remind him of a few things that happened during his regime as Postmaster General, when we used to have a few words to say in the House.

I am quite ready to wait until the Bill is printed, but at first sight, I say that you are increasing the rates per zone. That is how I read the resolution, and whilst a certain rate will prevail in one zone, the same rate will not prevail in another zone.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is not so.

So much the better if I am mistaken, but I read the resolution that way, and I will wait until the Bill is printed. But if I am in error, I am in error in company with many journalists, because, as former Postmaster General, I have been showered with protests from all parts of Canada against the resolution which has been presented this evening.

Probably they are
reading your own papers.
How does this resolution affect the transportation of magazines?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
A magazine is not
regarded specifically as a magazine; it comes under the newspaper class. Has my hon friend (Mr. Lemieux) concluded his remarks?
No. My hon. friend says that the rate is not raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I never said so at all. 1 explained that the rate was raised, and I thought I explained it in fairly clear English. I said that no zone system was established except in so far as it has always been established, even during my hon. friend's regime, in the forty mile limit for weekly newspapers.

Clause 3 reads:
That subsections two and three of section fifty-three of the said Act, as amended by section five of chapter fifty-three of the statutes of 1908, be repealed, and the following substituted therefor:-
(2) Newspapers and periodicals required to be transmitted by mail within a distance of forty miles from the place of publication, the publication of which is of no greater frequency than once a week, which have a circulation by mail of not more than one thousand copies per issue, and which are published in any city, town or village which has a population of not more, than five thousand persons, shall be transmitted free of postage within such area.



But without such area, what will be the rate?	*
(3) Newspapers and .periodicals which are required to be transmitted for a greater distance than is mentioned in the last preceding subsection-
Is not that another zone?
-or the publication of which is of greater frequency than once a week, shall be subject to postage at the rate of one cent-
There is an increase there.
-on and after the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-one, and until the first day of January, one thosand nine hundred and twenty-two, and one and one-half cents thereafter, for each pound weight or any fraction of a pound weight, and such postage shall be prepaid by postage stamps or otherwise as the Postmaster General from time to time directs.
My expression may be loose, but I am, * in essence, absolutely correct. You are raising the rate for passing from one district to another, if you prefer the word "district" to the word "zone", and you are adding six times the rate for passing from one district to the other. My hon. friend is playing upon words, and that is unworthy of him. I say that he is creating a zone system, and for passing from one zone to another he increased the rate. The journalists and newspaper proprietors know what they are talking about and they are protesting against this resolution, because they know that in the end they will have to pay the piper. What I am saying this evening-with some warmth, I agree-is on behalf of the real newspaper, the torch-bearer, not the advertisement monger. I am speaking for the real journalist, the real newspaper, the disseminator of news and knowledge as the word is defined in the Post Office Act. I agree that, for many years, many so-called newspapers have been transgressing the law, but it is the duty of the Postmaster General to prevent that. I regret that the Postmaster General is not in the House, and again I say that, precedent or no precedent-perhaps this is a hobby of mine-ministers who have a seat in the other chamber should, by the rules of Parliament, be allowed to appear before this assembly to explain their measures, just as ministers having a seat in this House should be' allowed to appear in the other chamber to explain their measures.
I think that reform has to come some day. As I said1 a moment ago, when the Bill is printed we shall have occasion to discuss this question further; but- I regret that the Government has come to the conclusion that knowledge, thought and education should be 
taxed. II was under the impression that having taxed almost everything they could think of, they would at least respect, those untaxable ethereal things such as knowledge, genius, art and public opinion as expressed by the writers in the press1. 1 think that on the whole, with very few exceptions, we have a clean press in Canada. On the whole, the periodicals of Canada are quite a credit to the country. In Toronto, in Montreal, in Halifax and in the (West there are periodicals which are a credit to this country. From what I can gather, the Canadian periodicals have an elevating effect on the public mind, and I cannot resist the temptation to read a letter which I have received bearing date May 12,	1920 from the
"Woman's Century, a national journal of education and progress .by Canadian women, and official organ of the National .Council of Women of Canada." I should like my hon. friend to listen to this letter, because it is most important and has a special hearing on this, question. With the cost of newsprint as it is, and with the high cost of living and the increase in wages, the task of publishing a newspaper or periodical to-day bears very heavily on the shoulders of the poor publisher. The letter I have received' is as follew-s:
Dear Sir:	I see that the Hon. Mr. Burrell,
Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue, has given notice of a resolution to be moved in the House regarding an increase in postage rates on newspapers, magazines, etc.
As President of the Womans' Century, I wish to point out certain things which I would beg you to take into very serious consideration on behalf of this publication and of the work that it is doing.
The magazine was launched in 1914 and has gone steadily forward in spite of the serious years of war and reconstruction. It is the organ of several national and provincial women's organizations throughout the Dominion and has a large circulation amongst women of all types. Its great object has been to educate womeD along social lines, to give them a good, stable understanding of public questions, and to put before them certain ideals for the nation. To this end such methods as "Made-in-Canada" programmes, child welfare, public health, Can-adianization and many other kindred subjects have received very constant and careful. attention.
During the reconstruction period we have had articles appealing to the women to use their influence in steadying our national life and in opposing any form of unconstitutional movement or Bolshevism. That the paper is doing fine work is proved by constant letters of appreciation and interests from people all over the Dominion and outside it.
If this bill should be passed, this good work would be very seriously hampered, and I feel one of the contributions that women are giving to the national life would suffer a kind of defeat.
I trust that you will be able to give your serious consideration and do all in your power

to help such magazines as this over the threatened danger. 1 might add that should magazines of this type be cut down, then there would be an incoming of American magazines with non-Canadian ideals, which in my opinion would be most dangerous to our country.
Yours sincerely,
Constance E. Hamilton, President, Woman's Century Limited.
I trust my hon. friend will pay attention to this appeal and take into due consideration the statements which are made in the letter. Now, let me tell my hon. friend that this increased tax on newspapers and periodicals will reduce the circulation of our Canadian periodicals and may .bring some of them under the hammer. This tax may drive them to the wall, and it certainly will prevent this campaign of Canadianization which .is mentioned in Madame Hamilton's letter, while the wealthy newspapers of the United States, including the Hearst publications, will flood our country. Already, Mr. Chairman, the people of Toronto are protesting vehemently against the inroads of such publications as the Hearst journals. The United States can dump their newspapers into Canada just, as before the anti-dumping legislation of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), they dumped their excess goods here. They can dump their newspapers and their periodicals, and jam the postal cards with their yellow literature. Of course, Mr. Chairman, I am not speaking of such newspapers as the New York Post and the Tribune, or such periodicals as The Century, the Atlantic Magazine or Munsey's. I do not refer to such publications, but I am speaking of the ugly, yellow American magazine. By this legislation you are precluding our own people from publishing and circulating clean .Canadian literature and clean Canadian thought and ideals, while you are opening the door to a flood of Yankee yellow literature.

I may as well confess at once that I happen to be personally interested in this resolution and I think it might be well if I placed before the committee the view of the Canadian daily newspapers, First of all, I will admit that when the question of postal rates came up they proposed an increase of their own which they were prepared to accept. The daily newspapers of Canada throught their association are in favour of a certain increase in postal rates, for the reason that they do not feel that the newspapers of Canada should be blamed for any deficit that might exist in the Postal Department. They do not claim that the increase will overcome 2131
that deficit, but they do not want the newspapers to be regarded as one of the causes of the deficit. The association met a month or more ago and conferred with the Postmaster-General and the Deputy Postmaster-General and proposed that the first increase should be from one-quarter cent to one-half cent. I know that the present proposal is not agreeable to many newspapers because they cannot meet such a heavy increase at once. They would rather have the increase from a quarter to a half in the beginning of next year, then an increase to a cent, and then an increase to a cent and a half if necessary. They take the ground that they do not want to be treated by the Post Office Department or the Country as a charitable institution.
That is the case now.

I may point out that a newspaper that has to meet an increased cost of this character cannot place it immediately on their customers. Subscriptions have been taken from the 1st of January this year up to the present time, and they apply for two years, and until that time the rates cannot be raised in respect of persons who have subscribed so far. These increased costs will eventually mean increased subscription rates; there is no doubt about that. In Alberta at the present time, owing to the rising cost of newsprint and the proposed increase in postal rates, the newspapers of Calgary and Edmonton have increased their rate to 25 cents a week for papers delivered in those cities, a matter of $13 a year, and to outside points the subscription has been raised from $5 to $8. They are starting out to meet the increased cost that will surely have to come to all the newspapers in Canada. These rising costs they must meet by increased subscription and advertising rates. I am not asking the Government not to make any increase at all; I am quite agreeable to an increase, but I think it should be graded a little differently front what is proposed here. I would not pbject of the cent rate were put into effect later but newspaper men think that a 300 per cent increase is pretty heavy to start with. If we were to start with a half a cent, then increase to a sent and then to a cent and a half later, they might make it up on their extra costs.
I might say in behalf of the newspaper publishers that the situation is extremely serious among the newspapers of the country largely due to the increased cost of newsprint. Prior to the war newsprint was selling at $40 a ton. It will be $80 to the end
[DOT]3354

of June, but it is going up to $120 the beginning of July. These costs, postal rates and all, have to be met. If the burden were made a little less at the present time and were increased gradually I do not think there would be any objection from the Canadian daily, newspaper publishers. They did meet the Postmaster General and were agreeable to an increase of half a cent. They would like that increase to be put into effect first and that the other rates should be imposed in six months or a year if necessary. I thought it might be worth while for the committee to understand the attitude of the daily newspaper publishers and that is the reason why I have made this statement on the question.

I am
thoroughly in accord with the spirit of this resolution. Although I am directly, or indirectly, associated with the publication of newspapers I do not see why the Government should carry my newspapers or any other people's newspapers for nothing. It is an absolute business transaction and we have the postal department running behind to the extent of $7,000,000 a year. This is not business. We could stand it probably in pre-war days and have some excuse for it but to-day, when we have to exert ourselves to the very utmost, and to impose taxation to the limit, I do not see why we have any reason to carry on a department of this Government in such an unbusinesslike way. If it is true, as has been said, that there are hundreds of employees in different parts of this department that are useless, for goodness sake, let us get down to the time when we can run every department of this Government on a business basis-lop off the mouldering branches, get new methods if necessary and new men and let us put this country on a paying basis. Probably I have not the same respect for free thought that some hon. members have. I am very doubtful if the newspapers of this country contribute very muph to it. The Associated Press is a great distributor of news and that goes over the wires. It is not transmitted by the mails. As far as the editorials are' concerned, I think they reflect to a great extent the opinions of one man and that man is the editor, whoever he may be. This is a public matter; we are here to look after the business of the people of Canada; and what right have we to carry newspapers to the extent of $6,000,000 or $7,000,000 a year for nothing, at a time when we are imposing taxation on the people? If newspapers cannot carry on at the present rates they have their remedy the

same as any other business man has; let them increase their advertising and circulation rates and not come down here and ask this Government to dole out charity to anybody. We are here to conduct the business of Canada in a business way and I hope the minister will go farther than the resolution specifies. I do not know why weekly newspapers should be carried free. They should carry a legitimate charge for transmitting their knowledge. Newspaper publication is a business; the publishers are conducting that business for a personal gain and profit. I have never yet seen any great philantrophy among the newspaper men and . publishers of this country; it is absolutely cold business; and it is up to this Government to conduct the business of this country in such a cold-blooded manner as to make the business of the country pay as we go. Canada is heavily in debt. The Lord knows we have to impose burdens enough on the people, and I do not think any appeal to charity is at the present time in order.

I want to say a word now, reserving until later whatever remarks I shall have to make on this subject. I understand that the purpose of this resolution is to get revenue, and such being the case probably the service of the department could be improved. I would call the attention of the minister to the fact that when a holiday falls on Monday the distribution of the mails in the cities is not made from Saturday noon till the next Tuesday which causes a good deal of damage to trade generally. My attention has been called by associations of merchants and all kinds of persons to this matter and I hope the minister will take it up with the department, and that the public in general will have reason to appreciate his intervention.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
In answer to my hon.
friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) who brought to my attention the fact that a thousand in regard to the weekly newspaper was a somewhat low figure for circulation free and that it should be extended to two thousand, there is a good deal in what he says. Now, I shall be personally very glad to give the maitter consideration and I think we may take that up when the Bill is introduced. My hon. friend from Resti-gouche and Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) touched on the same question but he went somewhat farther and argued that as a matter of principle papers such as those that he referred to should be allowed free mailing privileges altogether. I do not

know on what principle we could lay it down that newspapers of any kind should be allowed to pass through the mails free. If we carried that out to its logical conclusion, as my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Mo-Gibbon) has pointed out, the rest of the people who are not interested in these papers would be subsidizing them out of their own pockets. However, I shall be glad to give consideration to the question of the weekly newspaper and take it up on the second reading.
I would like to say a word or two in answer to the hon. member for .Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux), whose remarks, I must confess rather asitonished me. I am not going to follow him in his remarks about what was prior to 1896 the excellence of the administration of the department and the unfortunate depravity since that time, because I do not think it would be w.orth while going into that question. All the reforms which my hon. friend, or his predecessor, put into effect ought to make us rejoice, and if there was a complete absence of all kinds of abuses during the administration he can take comfort to his soul that such was the case, although I think that probably I could pick some flaws,-however, I shall not go into that question. I can say, however, that if there is a tremendous extension and an increase in the number of employees far in excess of what is absolutely justified by the service. I am sure that every member of this House, I do not care on which side he sits, will feel that such an increase should be wiped out of existence and that the service should be put upon a basis of business efficiency. In that the hon. gentleman does not feel any more -strongly than I do myself.
May I say a word about my hon. friend's remarks, the'tone of which I thought was entirely uncalled-for. He speaks about this part of the resolution being a "tax on free thought." It is not a question of a tax; it is a question of trying to make up from the users of the mail something of the enormous deficit which imposes a burden on the whole country. It is not a question of taxing free thought, it is asking the newspapers whose business results in a loss of some four or five million a year to the Government to bear a somewhat heavier share of the cost in order that we may at least do something towards making up the deficit. If my hon. friend can construe that into an attempt to tax thought we will never agree on a definition of what a tax is. My hon. friend asked us to seriously consider before we take that step, but I wish he had considered this
thing a little more himself. He is absolutely wrong when he talks about a zone system in referring to the forty-mile district in which a weekly newspaper may be carried free.
Mr. LEMilEUX:	What would you call
it?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
That is the forty-mile
district for a weekly newspaper, but what my hon. friend has in his mind is that the newspapers which have been writing to him and to me were afraid that there was going to be what is known generally as the zone system, namely, that beyond a 300-mile line there was going to be an additional charge. That is what is known to the newspaper men as the zone system, That zone system is not in this resolution, but the forty mile limit for weekly newspapers is precisely as it was under the old administration, except that we ask that from the central point of publication the distance shall not exceed forty miles.

That does not apply to
dailies.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Not to dailies. There is some misapprehension as to that. My hon. friend talks eloquently about the sword of the ancestor of the hon. member for North Simcoe and so on. I am not going to follow him in anything of that kind. But there was one other thing the hon. member said he would like to touch on. He said that he himself was here as an advocate of those high exemplars of thought in the newspaper world, the torchdoearers as he called them, and he seemed to have some extraordinary idea that we were encouraging all the worst forms of the press and were suppressing in some mysterious way the "torch-bearers" that he alluded to. Well, I will just say that our definition of the press is precisely what was in the Revised Statutes in 1906 and was in effect in my hon. friend's regime. Paragraph (a) of section 53 of the old Act reads that:
A newspaper is known and recognized as a newspaper or periodical in the general sense of the word, and consists wholly or in great part of political or other news, or of articles relative thereto, or on other current topics, and is published regularly at intervals of not more than one month.
Now it is no good for my hon. friend to talk about "suppressing" the "torch-bearers." .There is a definition of a newspaper that existed in the Act when my hon. friend was Postmaster General, and it is precisely that definition under which we are working

to-day, and there is no proposal to change it. I may say that we do require a reasonable and proper amount of reading matter and political and other news, before the publication can be classed as a newspaper, and get the benefit of these rates, because it was not thought desirable that papers should go out with an overwhelming mass of advertising and a minimum of news.
Now in reference to this whole matter, if my hon. friend has any other thoughts that would bear more directly on the question than those he has expressed to-night, or any suggestions to make, I need hardly say-as the minister who is piloting the Bill through this House-that I would be only too glad to give them the greatest consideration. I must, however, take a strong exception to his view of this proposal to try and see that the newspapers of the country pay at least a little more than they have been paying towards the very heavy load which we have been carrying for them, and I must deprecate his citing that as "attacks on free thought'' in any shape or form.
I may say in answer to my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) that I know the views he has placed before the committee to-night are the views that have been expressed from a great many quarters in Canada to me-and I suppose to the Postmaster General-during the last few weeks. I am quite aware that the newspapers are facing somewhat hard conditions in regard to their supply of newsprint and its increased cost. At the same time whatever is finally decided-whether we adhere to the provisions of the resolutions and the provisions of the Bill which is to be founded upon those resolutions or whether there is any modification-what I have stated before must not be forgotten, that even whatever amount we do advance these charges by, owing to the necessary increase in the railway charges which is bound to come, the department and the country-because the department represents the country-will be facing an enormous deficit even if you charge up to one cent. However, I think that matter could better be discussed at a later stage.

I would like to get the
figures of the cost of carrying these newspapers, and what revenue we propose to get from that. The minister has stated that we are carrying 87,000,000 pounds of paper at the present time, and the revenue derived therefrom is $290,000. He proposes

to impose a rate of four times the present amount, and even that increase will not pay the cost of handling. I would like to get the exact figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: It would be difficult to give the figures with any absolute exactitude to-night. I have given a rough estimate for the purpose of explaining the general sense of the resolutions. I could give the figures more accurately when the Bill which is to be founded on the resolutions comes up for second reading. It is right, as my hon. friend states, that we charge a quarter of a cent a pound for carrying newspapers at present. The revenue from this source has been about $291,000, and the extent of the loss entailed by the carrying of these newspapers is estimated to be pretty close to $5,000,000. Under the terms of the resolution the rate for carriage is increased from a quarter of a cent to one cent per pound, tout even if that proposal is carried out it will certainly he very far from meeting anything Kke the expenditure involved.

Is the minister prepared to give the committee the amount that is lost on the distribution of catalogues and also on the carriage of parcels? I understand there is an annual loss of from twenty to thirty millions in the carrying of parcels for the departmental stores, figured on the same basis as that for the carriage of newspapers?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit me I will give that information upon the second reading of the Bill. I will say in passing that I am quite aware that while there may be differences of opinion with respect to certain provisions in these resolutions there is no necessity for altering the resolutions now. Nor is there any grave reason why the passage of the resolutions should be delayed. I am giving a running explanation of their purpose in order that when the Bill comes before the House all the varying views that members may entertain may be advanced perhps with greater effect. I will finish, therefore, with a comment on the other clauses.
It is proposed to repeal the old sections 75, 76, 79 and 81 which deal with the question of franking, and to substitute certain other clauses which in the main amount to this: Whereas in the past it was customary not only for all departmental literature and letters, and mailable matter of all kinds, to be sent from the seat of Government by departments, and by members and senat-

ors, it was also customary for all mailable matter and letters addressed to any department of government by a member to come in free. That part is deleted, and while the privilege is retained of franking departmental literature and government publications, and members' mailable matter and letters, being still franked out they will not come in free. I think myself that this is a wholesome.reform because there has been a tremendous abuse of the franking privilege generally, and certainly a very great loss of revenue. The franking privilege hitherto enjoyed by the provinces for the distribution of all their government publications is also cut out. There are hundreds of tons of government publications in the various provinces going out free, and the department thought there was really no reason why the Dominion Government and the people of Canada from a federal standpoint, should carry free the mails of a province, when, after all, each province is perfectly able to attend to that matter itself.
I might mention that a penalty is provided for the franking of matter that does not deal with the personal affairs of a member or senator. I think I am well within the mark when I say that the franking privilege by members has been abused, not so much willingly by the member himself as by all sorts of pressure from other people who got him to frank their letters and he himself was not in the position-without being extremely ungracious-of refusing them, although the course in question certainly was not justified. This simply gives him a reason by which he can say to anybody, "1 am not permitted under the law-a violation of which will lay me open to a penalty-to frank your letters, or the letters of your friends' friends at the public expense simply because you are my friend." The changes proposed will cut that practice out. I need only give an illustration of the abuse of this privilege by saying that years ago when members of the Civil Service were allowed to frank their letters a boarding house in Ottawa advertised its advantages as such by reason of the fact that it had civil servants there, and that those civil servants would frank all the letters of the people who came to the house. There were also times in the old days when members came to Ottawa and found that it was a very expensive business to do their laundry here and so franked their washing home, got it done there and then brought it back. I remember an instance related by the late Sir Hector Langevin that when he was Minister of Public Works at one time they could take down to the station in a small bag the mail matter franked from the Department of Public Works. Suddenly there was an
enormous increase and they found there were merchants and other people coming into the department and unloading whole truck-loads of stuff there because all the departmental matter went through the mails free. In England the abuse was equally flagrant, in fact the system was abused to such an extent that members were known to frank even pianos down to their constituencies. It led in England to the wiping out of the whole privilege. Although that policy has since been reversed, the privilege has been greatly restricted. Here, in the public interest, we are going to at least wipe out the greater abuses in connection with the franking privilege. I think that is all I need say in comment on the resolutions.
Is it proposed to preclude the franking of campaign literature?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I would not say that, because as I understand the resolutions anything to do with the business of the Government, or public business, goes free. I take it for granted that my hon. friend would not send out as campaign literature anything that did not deal with public business.

I would like to ask a question of the minister with reference to the franking privilege. I notice that in subsection 2 of section 76 it is declared:
All letters posted for transmission under this section must be franked by the personally written signature of the member of the Senate or of the House of Commons sending the same.
Does that mean that we shall not be permitted to frank by our^initials?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I would not like to
speak positively on that point. I think the view of the department is that the initial franking has been very much abused; and, strictly speaking, a frank should be a signature. The latter method is a very much greater protection to the department. On the other hand, I think the question might well be dealt with, and I will find out further about it.

The written signature is
specified here in the same clause. Lots of members have often in the neighbourhood of 200 letters a day, and to have to sit down and sign that number of envelopes is a nuisance. In addition it would preclude
.3358

issuing a number of circular letters to a member's constituents. Why not change the wording so that a member's personal stamp could be adopted in lieu of his signature?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The facsimile can be
used on all mailable matter.
That is only on open mail other than letters.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Yes. It may be a
hardship. On the other hand, I know when I was Secretary of State I personally had to sign my signature to far more than 200 or 300 certificates of naturalization, company charters, and so on.
Is printed matter enclosed in an envelope a "letter"?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I presume it would be
if sealed.

Most of the printed
matter that goes out is in closed envelopes.

When the stamp rate was raised from 2 to 3 cents as a war tax, the question of whether or not a constituent sending letters to' his member would have to stamp them was raised, and I have a distinct recollection of the then Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) holding that it was in the public interest that the communication with a member should be kept free. I am disappointed to find that the privilege is being removed. I do not know why this change of policy has been adopted by the same Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Is my hon. friend drawing a distinction only so far as letters addressed to members are concerned? He does not suggest that letters addressed to all departments of government should be free? My hon. friend will understand that an enormous number of inquiries are sent in to the various departments, and in ordinary cases it would be worth a man's while if the information he is inquiring about is of any value to him at all to affix a three-cent stamp to his letter. The floods of correspondence of that kind entail a very heavy loss of revenue. However, this point can be taken up.
That point was raised on the occasion I refer to.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It can be given consideration.
Resolution reported without amendment and concurred in.

Mr. BURRELL thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 167 to amend the Post Office Act.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.
On motion of Rt. Hon. Mr. Doherty, the House adjourned at 12.10 a.m. (Thursday).
Thursday, June 10, 1920.
